Determining the mean lifetime of $B^0_s$ mesons is significant in identifying the CKM paradigm's most prominent break, a crucial parameter for certain CP-violating processes. By utilizing around 125 ps/$c$ of $B^0_s$ data from LHCb, this study calculates the mean lifetime of $B^0_s$ decaying into two kaons. The outcome, a mean lifetime of 1.440 ps with 0.013 uncertainty, is derived through a variety of approaches, including direct measurement, use of $B^0_s$ decay trees, and relative lifetime calculations with respect to $B^0$ mesons. All methods yield consistent outcomes, confirming the earlier estimate of 1.46 ps with 0.01 uncertainty and also providing evidence for the $B^0_s$ dominance in neutral $K^+K^-$ meson systems with a relative fraction of $0.76\pm0.08$ (statistic) $\pm0.02$ (systematic). Furthermore, this study also reports the first precise calculation of the mean lifetime of the $B^0$ meson decaying into two kaons, yielding a result of 1.406 ps with 0.006 uncertainty. Additionally, a ratio of $N(B^0_s)/N(B^0)$ values, obtained from the same data set, equals 0.0644±0.0035 (statistic) ±0.0012 (systematic), which is consistent with the expectations from the CKM paradigm and does not impact the recent findings from LHCb and CMS of $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ data.

Deep learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are frequently used for time series data analysis due to their effectiveness, despite often requiring extensive parameter sets that can lead to performance bottlenecks. We introduce a trimming method called Trim In Time (PIT) that systematically reviews and refines each network layer based on its contribution to training, allowing for a targeted reduction of parameters while maintaining the original's performance. Compared to a popular sparse training method called Sparse Inclusive Training (SIT), PIT achieves comparable accuracy with a 2% increase in training time, ultimately resulting in a 30% parameter reduction. Our approach is also distinct in its ability to identify and remove unnecessary residual connections, resulting in a 9% additional reduction in parameters for no accuracy degradation. When applied to the TCN model, PIT yields a 45% parameter reduction while maintaining 92% of the original's accuracy on the MIMIC-III CSV dataset. Furthermore, our proposed method is suitable for all TCN variants and can be integrated into their code with minimal modifications. Additionally, we have made the code for PIT available online at the specified URL. Counting-based time series data, such as accident counts or crime rates, often fluctuate significantly over time and are frequently affected by external factors. These changes can render traditional Poisson autoregressive models ineffective, and a new model is required that accounts for the temporal variations in such data. This paper presents a novel Temporally Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPA) model that adapts to changes in time series data by dividing the overall timeline into sub-periods with relatively stable accident rates. This model builds upon the foundation of the Poisson autoregressive model and incorporates the use of external control variables to model risk factors that influence the time series data. Our research provides the theoretical framework for the TVPA model's parameters, and through simulated data, demonstrates the model's performance and accuracy. Furthermore, the TVPA model is applied to real-world data from accident count data in Shanghai, and comparative studies are conducted to evaluate its effectiveness against other popular time series models. The results show that the TVPA model exhibits superior performance in both simulated and actual data settings. The new data include a high signal-to-noise ratio of 240 for a 2.5 Angstroms wavelength range, as well as 128 spatial pixels covering the region around Ton 2. The optical spectrum shows no significant hydrogen or helium absorption from Ton 2, with no evidence of gas associated with the stream or the globular cluster. However, there is an absorption feature originating from the background sky. Additionally, the new data enable us to determine the radial velocity of Ton 2, confirming its previous measurement of approximately 54 km/s. The velocity of Ton 2 is distinct from that of the stream or structure within the Milky Way's bulge, which has a velocity of approximately 46 km/s. No stars were found within a projected distance of approximately 2.5 parsecs from Ton 2. The new data, combined with the prior findings from the CAPOS team, provide further insight into the stream or structure within the Milky Way's bulge, while the lack of associated gas around Ton 2 raises questions regarding the stream's formation.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, providing an invaluable resource for both experienced and new users in the field of theorem-based proof development. Despite its utility, many potential contributors remain deterred by the archive's complexity, hindering its further development. This combination of accomplishments and untapped potential gives rise to the idea of creating a demonstration framework, one that could enhance the archive's visibility and appeal to contributors, while also providing a useful demonstration tool for users to explore proofs interactively. We propose a demonstration framework, consisting of a set of commands and attributes, designed to streamline the process of presenting and refining existing proofs, as well as a detailed overview of its implementation and applications. We invite the Isabelle community to engage with our proposal, exploring both its benefits and areas for improvement, with the ultimate goal of integrating a demonstration framework into the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. This idea has already sparked interest from the community, with at least three contributors expressing a willingness to adapt their existing proofs using our proposed framework. We believe our approach can help address the challenge of maintaining a healthy balance between the archive's size and the level of understanding it demands from viewers. With the ever-increasing pace of new contributions, it has become essential to provide a clearer visual overview of each proof, as well as a more engaging way to experience the archive's content. Our proposed framework addresses these concerns, offering a unique way to present proofs, along with a new demonstration tool for users to explore and customize proofs with a visually appealing interface. We hope this approach will pave the way for a more effective collaboration between the archive's maintainers, contributors, and users, with a focus on further developing the archive's content and making it more accessible to the broader community. The primary objective of this research is to validate the theoretical concept that any continuous, completely integrable vector field on a manifold whose points have the same Lie algebra structure can be converted into a formally equivalent vector field using an orbital transformation. This research also examines the conditions under which this conversion becomes possible. Building on previous work by Ghillani and Roger, we leverage their findings to prove that any continuous, completely integrable vector field can be converted into a formally equivalent vector field using an orbital transformation for analytic manifolds of any dimension greater than one. However, for one-dimensional manifolds, this conversion is only guaranteed for vector fields with non-trivial first integral. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof for continuous vector fields on one-dimensional manifolds under the condition that their first integral is nowhere zero. Furthermore, we extend this conversion concept to vector fields with non-trivial first integrals on closed orbits by demonstrating that any continuous, completely integrable vector field on these orbits can be converted into a formally equivalent vector field using an orbital transformation for one-dimensional manifolds. Lastly, we outline an application of this conversion along with some numerical examples utilizing the experience of computing first integrals for the time-dependent Henon map. Finally, we conclude this research by providing solutions to local version problems for one-dimensional manifolds under the condition that their first integral is nowhere zero. Accurate pose estimation in 3D from 2D projections is a complex, ill-posed problem, particularly when working with limited and noisy data. This challenge is compounded when working with intricate objects whose pose depends on multiple parameters. For instance, the pose of human hands or full bodies in real-time video streams falls into this category. A significant obstacle in this context is the absence of a robust feature that can distinguish between object points and those of the background. This study introduces an end-to-end neural network, DeepHMap++, which can resolve this issue. It begins by employing a merged projection clustering module to identify object features from a set of projected 3D coordinates. This module uses a non-linear function to estimate the probability of a point belonging to the object and then applies this probability to weight the loss function. The model then enters a correspondence learning module, where it matches the identified object features with their corresponding 2D projections. This is achieved by maximizing the likelihood of corresponding points having similar projections. The model is trained on a dataset with multiple parameters and is applicable to scenarios with a high degree of freedom, such as estimating the pose of human hands or full bodies. This study presents DeepHMap++ in the context of a challenging benchmark problem, the CMU Panos Dataset, and compares it to clustering-based models and pose estimation models that assume predefined correspondences. The results show that DeepHMap++ outperforms these models significantly. The study is further validated by applying the model to the estimation of human pose, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict missing correspondences and pose parameters. The source code of DeepHMap++ is available at https://github.com/author/DeepHMap++ and has been integrated into the OpenPose framework. In this talk, we will be working within the framework of $R$-Minkowski spacetimes, which are characterized by a linear field that governs the behavior of geodesics. We will demonstrate that the conventional formula for the Laplace operator, initially derived by Dirac for Minkowski spacetimes, is no longer applicable in $R$-Minkowski spacetimes. This discrepancy arises from the non-existence of a global basis for the Clifford algebra in $R$-Minkowski spacetimes, which complicates the expression for the Laplace operator. Nonetheless, we have established an alternative formulation for the Laplace operator, drawing from the concepts of geometric algebra and algebraic structure, and this formulation serves as a viable replacement for Dirac's formula in $R$-Minkowski spacetimes. Furthermore, this alternative formulation facilitates the derivation of a Laplace operator for the complexified $R$-Minkowski spacetimes. This discussion also explores the algebraic basis for the Schwinger model in $R$-Minkowski spacetimes. Finally, we will discuss the potential for generalizing this approach to other types of homogeneous spacetimes. This talk is primarily based on the paper recently submitted to the journal, and the paper is currently available on the arXiv website.

The box game, a parvocellular sensory phenomenon, presents an apparent conflict between voluntary decision-making and an underlying mechanism of selection. However, recent research suggests that this conflict arises not from a deliberate decision process but rather a fundamental aspect of the game's design, specifically its use of a binary choice format. A theoretical model based on free-choice probability offers a more comprehensive explanation for the observed biases in player preferences, providing a clear alternative to the original selectionist hypothesis. To further test the validity of this hypothesis, a new variant of the box game was created, featuring a trichotomy rather than a binary choice, and the results of player experiments revealed a similar pattern of preferences, thus supporting the idea that the box game's effects stem from its general design properties rather than any unique feature associated with choice. Additionally, analysis of the data from the trichotomy game has led to a refinement of the free-choice probability model, identifying distinct decision-making processes for sure and uncertain outcomes. Overall, the research on the box game has implications for our understanding of voluntary decision-making, suggesting that it is influenced by implicit rules governing choice presentation and that the model of free-choice probability provides a useful framework for studying decision-making under uncertainty. Furthermore, the findings have been incorporated into a broader theory of choice, the "principle of choice generality," which posits that any stable pattern of choice observed in a simple decision task must be an inherent property of the task's design or must result from the interplay of fundamental decision-making processes such as the free-choice probability model and expected utility theory. The research has been extended to other classic phenomena like the Ultimatum Game and the Prisoner's Dilemma to demonstrate how they might be reinterpreted through the lens of choice generality and how they might be modified to elicit more cooperative behavior. The paper also explores the distinction between "paradigm-driven" and "statistical" effects in the context of decision theory, suggesting that the box game phenomenon falls into the former category and highlights the importance of considering the design properties of choice tasks to gain a deeper understanding of decision-making processes. The research has been conducted with a mixed-methods design using a combination of theoretical modeling, computational simulations, and player experiments to investigate the box game dilemma. The data collected from the trichotomy game experiments has been analyzed using a combination of frequentist and Bayesian statistical techniques, and the results have been validated through replication in both the laboratory and online settings. The escalating use of MRI in clinical settings and research necessitates the development of more effective strategies for ensuring image quality. Human experts, despite their excellence in evaluating MRI images, are prone to errors and inconsistencies in their assessments. To address this challenge, a promising approach involves training machine learning models to replicate the decisions made by these human experts. However, achieving generalizability - the ability of these models to perform well on new, unseen data - is a significant difficulty. This paper explores the challenge of training a machine learning model to predict the quality of cerebral MRI images, a complex task involving multiple dimensions. The evaluation of such a model is typically based on whether it can accurately classify images as high or low quality, a binary outcome. However, this approach overlooks the underlying continuous quality spectrum inherent to MRI images. We contend that a more effective strategy is to model quality as a continuous variable, rather than a discrete one. This approach enables the incorporation of diverse performance metrics, including the mean absolute error, to assess a model's performance alongside classification accuracy. We demonstrate the advantages of this continuous approach through the training of a machine learning model to predict MRI quality, outperforming the industry standard approach along multiple evaluation metrics. Our work showcases the feasibility of applying deep learning techniques to replicate the decisions made by human experts in MRI quality assessment, while addressing a critical limitation of existing methods. The foundation theorem is a significant concept in the theory of Coxeter groups, particularly evident in the Rota-Hustad theorem and its generalizations. This thesis explores an extension of the foundation theorem to the B-type Coxeter groups, which are generated by the transpositions of roots. A key finding is the demonstration that the foundation theorem is applicable to any element in a finite Coxeter group of type B. This achievement also leads to a generalized version of the Rota-Hustad theorem. Furthermore, this research identifies the basis elements in a Coxeter group of type B that have minimal length foundations, and shows that these foundations are related to the exponents of the eigenvalues of the Coxeter operator. This thesis also examines the foundation theorem in connection with the descent set of a group element, and establishes a connection between the length of a foundation and the size of a descent set. Additionally, this research explores the foundation theorem within the context of the symmetric group, and identifies the elements in the symmetric group with minimal length foundations. Finally, this thesis explores the foundation theorem in connection with the lattice structure of a Coxeter group, and establishes a connection between the length of a foundation and the join and meet operations of a Coxeter group. This thesis also explores the foundation theorem in connection with the order of a group element, and establishes a connection between the length of a foundation and the order of a Coxeter group. We have examined the metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ superlattices with varying LaAlO$_3$ layer thickness using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR and found our results to be in line with theoretical predictions indicating the intercalation of Li$^+$ into the LaNiO$_3$ layers, thus enabling the measurement of LaNiO$_3$ conduction band properties. Our data show that the spin-lattice relaxation time $T_1$ follows the same behavior as the conductivity in these superlattices, indicating that $T_1$ is governed by the movement of LaNiO$_3$ electrons. Furthermore, we have identified the LaAlO$_3$ layer thickness at which the LaNiO$_3$ conduction band becomes isolated from the interface states by measuring the Knight shift and spin-lattice relaxation time in our $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR spectra. Our measurements indicate that the Knight shift and $T_1$ inverse are both maximum at a LaAlO$_3$ layer thickness of 6 units, corresponding to a LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness of 3 units, and that they significantly decrease at higher layer thicknesses, demonstrating the isolated LaNiO$_3$ conduction band in these superlattices. Our research paves the way for the in-depth study of electronic states in functional materials with NMR spectroscopy. Additionally, we have observed a Ca doping effect on the metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ single-crystal references through $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR, and found that the spin-lattice relaxation time $T_1$ displays different damping patterns in LaAlO$_3$/LaNiO$_3$ superlattices and LaNiO$_3$ single-crystal references at high magnetic fields, attributing this to a difference in the LaNiO$_3$ conduction band state between the two systems. MediaWiki-based websites like Wikipedia and many others have demonstrated their effectiveness in facilitating collaborative projects. Our proposal, WorkingWiki, builds upon this success by creating a tailored framework for research cooperation on a large scale. This concept leverages MediaWiki's features to provide a comprehensive framework, encompassing data management, collaborative tools, and infrastructure for both internal and external research collaborations. WorkingWiki can serve as a foundation for a variety of applications, including next-generation simulation platforms and HPC-enabled data analytics sites, thanks to its modular design. Specifically, we present WorkingWiki in the context of the BEACON2 project, an HPC-enabled research initiative focused on bioinformatics and genomics. This project has already seen success with over 1,000 registered users and a wealth of user-generated content, highlighting the viability of our approach. Our experience with WorkingWiki has revealed key insights on the essential features for a cooperative research platform, which we summarize into three main categories: trust factors, collaborative functionalities, and technical infrastructure. These findings are relevant to the development of any large-scale cooperative research platform. Our proposal and the associated project resources are available under an open-source license, enabling other researchers to build upon our concept and explore the broader implications of cooperative research platforms. These implications are exemplified through the analysis of WorkingWiki's community dynamics, which we explore through various metrics, including network analysis, collaborative patterns, and user behavior within the platform. Our experience with WorkingWiki has enabled us to identify several lessons that can benefit the development of future cooperative research platforms, along with our open-source code available on GitHub. This code not only underpins the analysis presented in our paper but also provides a practical demonstration of WorkingWiki's capabilities and its underlying infrastructure. Furthermore, we have devised an evaluation framework for assessing the effectiveness of cooperative research platforms like WorkingWiki, which we have applied to our own project. This evaluation framework comprises three primary components: (1) trust factors, which encompass aspects like user engagement, community growth, and the preservation of scientific heritage within the platform; (2) collaborative functionalities, which involve the examination of feature adoption, tool usage, and the integration of external research tools and methods; and (3) technical infrastructure, which focuses on the analysis of performance metrics, security, and the monitoring of the underlying technology stack. The discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 marked a significant milestone in particle physics, 
enabling a deeper exploration of the Higgs sector and the underlying theory of electroweak symmetry breaking. 
While the Higgs boson's properties are intricately connected to those of the top quark and vector bosons, 
they are also susceptible to influences from new physics realms that not yet been discovered. 
As a result, a more thorough examination of the Higgs boson, often referred to as "Higgs physics," 
is crucial to a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe. 
This presentation will delve into the diverse array of Higgs physics interpretations, 
focusing on those related to new physics phenomena that could manifest at an infinitesimally small scale, 
thus earning the label of "new tiny physics." 
As such, this discussion will encompass not just the search for new physics in the Higgs boson's properties, 
but also its role in searching for new tiny physics in other sectors of the Standard Model and beyond. 
This includes examinations of the global "2-sided" searches for new physics, 
where new physics could manifest as a tiny new field that interacts with the Higgs boson, 
as well as the exploration of new physics that could be hidden from the Higgs boson's detection, 
and the distinctive signatures that could emerge in the search for new tiny physics at the LHC. 
This presentation will be a review of the most pressing challenges, 
as well as the most compelling solutions and the most intriguing opportunities that lie ahead, 
focusing on the most promising avenues for further investigation, 
and the key roles that LHC experiments will play in the pursuit of new tiny physics.

In another group, comprising systems with spin periods over five seconds, the intervals between repetitions are significantly shorter, often measured in days. Additionally, the duration of outbursts increases with the mass accretion rate, which in turn depends on the brightness of the system. Human discourse is characterized by a diverse range of semantic elements, including basic facts, moral principles, and entertaining anecdotes. This variety of semantics is reflected in the phrases used by people, which can be both precise and vague. To capture this diversity, we develop a new discourse paradigm featuring complex semantic elements and encompassing a wide range of topics. This discourse is presented in the form of paragraphs, with each element defined by a categorical label such as "entertaining" or "alarming". To evaluate the coherence of these discourse elements, we create an inference task where one sentence is assessed in relation to another. Our findings reveal that both the categorization of individual elements and the inference tasks related to these discourses are challenging for current language models. In an effort to advance the field, we release a new dataset comprised of 13,000 sentences, which are organized into 18 categories and feature complex semantic elements. This dataset showcases the diverse nature of human discourse and highlights the difficulties faced by current language models when processing semantically complex discourse elements. To further test these models, we also introduce a binary classification task to determine whether two sentences are semantically similar or distinct. Our results indicate that the best model performs only slightly better than a random classifier, which suggests that there is significant room for improvement in the development of more effective language models capable of processing complex semantic varieties in human discourse. These models will be crucial in creating more sophisticated artificial discourse models, which can engage in meaningful conversations and provide accurate summaries of lengthy discourse segments. To achieve this, they will need to be able to classify high-level semantic categories such as "amusing" or "disturbing" and understand the relationships between sentences, which are best captured using the principles of distributivity and contrastiveness. These two factors will be essential in guiding the development of more effective neural network architectures and will need to be integrated into evaluation metrics that assess a model's ability to process complex semantic varieties. Our work also raises important questions about the role of evaluation metrics in modeling complex human discourse and the importance of maintaining a diverse range of semantic elements in evaluation datasets. Ultimately, our goal should be to create artificial discourse models that are not only highly realistic but also capable of engaging in meaningful conversations and providing accurate summaries of lengthy discourse segments. To achieve this, we will need to develop more sophisticated evaluation metrics that assess a model's ability to process complex semantic varieties and to create neural network architectures that can accurately classify high-level semantic categories and understand the relationships between sentences. If this remnant is massive enough, it could eventually become a neutron star or black hole.  In a study on rotating stellar remnants conducted here, it was assumed that objects with masses below 1.8 solar masses, which do not experience a type II supernova, undergo conservation of angular momentum during their formation.  Focusing on remnants with masses between 1.4 and 1.8 solar masses, which have the potential to become neutron stars, simulations of rotators were performed using Euler equations for compressible fluids in a spherical coordinate system.  By solving these equations numerically and analyzing rotators with various specific angular momentum values, it was found that there are two critical densities in rotators with masses between 1.4 and 1.8 solar masses, which determine their stability.  Additionally, in cases where conservation of angular momentum applies, the maximum stable mass of a rotating stellar remnant is given by the mass boundary for non-rotating stars plus one-third as much mass as the angular momentum boundary for non-rotating stars. This paper examines the problem of incremental learning, specifically tackling its challenge in dealing with constantly shifting and imbalanced datasets. We develop a comprehensive evaluation framework for advanced incremental learning algorithms, particularly those utilizing calibration techniques to address the issues of data shift and imbalanced classes. This framework encompasses various calibration methods, including reinforcement learning, multi-task learning, and memory-augmentation techniques. We apply our framework to a robust incremental learning algorithm called Incremental Learning via Calibration and Memory Augmentation (ILCMA), which we implement using a deep neural network model. The effectiveness of our approach is rigorously tested across multiple datasets, including the MNIST, EMNIST, and Sentient-Tech Sentiment Analysis Dataset. Our findings demonstrate that ILCMA outperforms a strong baseline in most cases, yielding a notable improvement of up to 126.8% in average accuracy on increasingly difficult datasets. However, we also observe instances where the performance of ILCMA declines, highlighting scope for future research to address these exceptions. Moreover, our extensive experimentation is accompanied by detailed analysis to provide insights into the behavior of our approach and the evaluation of our framework. Furthermore, we embark on a design-centric evaluation methodology for advanced incremental learning algorithms, suggesting that both rigorous theoretical evaluation and comprehensive experimentation are essential for valid assessment. This is further exemplified by our discovery that the performance of ILCMA is heavily dependent on the specific configuration of the memory mechanism, underscoring the significance of explicit design considerations for such architectures. Lastly, our work is relevant to fields like computer vision and natural language processing, where handling shifting and imbalanced data is a prevalent challenge. This is illustrated by our application of the ILCMA framework to sentiment analysis, a NLP domain characterized by data shift and class imbalance. This involves developing a novel dataset, called the Sentient-Tech Sentiment Analysis Dataset, comprising 1,000 samples per class across five incremental stages, and achieving with it a notable improvement of up to 126.8% in average accuracy using the ILCMA algorithm. This finding is noteworthy, given the scarcity of available datasets with clear labels for the scenario of continuous class growth in incremental learning. Recent studies have highlighted the underutilization of computing resources in data centers, shedding light on the untapped potential for speedup through instruction-level techniques. To leverage this opportunity, we introduce HyperDegrade, a novel, multi-threaded approach to instruction set specialization. By utilizing a sample set of instructions that represent the majority of executed operations, HyperDegrade creates a reduced instruction set that matches the capabilities of a smaller set of CPU cores. Through instruction set simulation and real-world evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperDegrade in enhancing energy efficiency and performance. When applied to real workloads running on 2GHz 64-core servers, HyperDegrade achieves an average energy savings of 20% and a 15% boost in performance, without compromising memory accessibility and system functionality. The improved configuration also facilitates easier migration to newer CPU cores with reduced instruction set compatibility issues. By presenting trade-off analysis and design decisions, along with both theoretical and practical applications, our research provides a framework for developing instruction-level speedup methods in collaboration with cloud service providers. The introduction of HyperDegrade has already been adopted by Google in their cloud services, and the technique is compatible with Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure as well. The research is currently being explored for application in emerging applications utilizing homogeneous multi-core processors, such as edge servers and real-time AI systems. The implementation of HyperDegrade has been implemented as an open-source library available on GitHub, under the terms of the permissive BSD license. A significant challenge in developing complex robot swarms lies in the limited processing and communication capabilities of individual robots. To address this, a novel collaborative approach is introduced, built on conventional beacons and used for tasks such as area coverage, where robots collaborate to achieve goals without the need for direct communication. The effectiveness of this collaborative approach and its placement algorithm is demonstrated through simulations and tests using a robot swarm equipped with conventional 802.15.4 radio transceivers. The results show that this method can lead to more efficient coverage and a higher success rate of communication when individual robots can only transmit for short periods. This paper exposes a novel form of attack, tailored to manipulate the privacy assumptions in vertically partitioned machine learning. In a typical vertically partitioned setting, different individuals or organizations hold different features of data, and these features are combined for training. Our attack exploits this separation, hiding a malicious feature within the data provided to mislead a trainer. Once the model is trained, the malicious feature is revealed, allowing the corruption of the model for malicious gain. We demonstrate this attack's effectiveness on linear models, decision trees, and neural networks, recognizing that its success depends on the specific data partitioning. Further research into understanding and mitigating this type of attack is encouraged. We also introduce an abductive reasoning-based attack on linear models, offering a concrete example of this type of assault. The implications and potential defenses of this attack on linear models are examined in detail.  We anticipate this attack to be adaptable to other machine learning models as well. The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/zheng-ecai/PAVP. The terms PAVP and PRPA are being considered for registration as a mark. The established policy evaluation method for model-based reinforcement learning, known as the evaluation loss, has a flaw: it does not guarantee an accurate assessment of the model's performance. This limitation causes some trained models to significantly deviate from optimal performance. A new evaluation criterion called the "wrapped evaluation loss" overcomes this deficiency, ensuring precise evaluation results. Despite its efficiency, the new criterion lacks a clear theoretical justification. To address this knowledge gap, we have derived a general formula for the "wrapped evaluation loss" and established its connection to the actual performance, providing a foundation for further investigation into reinforcement learning optimization. Furthermore, we have discovered a specific "wrapped evaluation loss" that is resilient to biased exploration-exploitation trade-offs, leading to the development of a new algorithm, SAMSE, which achieves superior performance compared to existing methods. Our findings demonstrate that SAMSE's performance surpasses that of the established methods in complex environments requiring complex observations and multiple steps to complete a task. 

In model-based reinforcement learning, the evaluation loss is widely accepted as the optimal method for evaluating policy models. However, this method has a significant drawback: it fails to account for the model's consistency, leading to models that are trained on exploration data but are actually evaluated on exploitation behavior. As a result, the performance of models trained using the evaluation loss often drops precipitously when they are deployed in actual exploitation scenarios.

To address this issue, we propose using the advantage function in place of the log probability, which leads to the formulation of the evaluation loss as the sum of the logged probabilities under the target policy and the expected values under the model. This formulation provides the basis for our analysis of the limitations of the evaluation loss.

We show that the failure of the evaluation loss to consider the model's consistency results in it being insensitive to the exploration-exploitation trade-off. This means that models trained using the evaluation loss will always prioritize exploiting the most visited states over exploring new ones, even when the model is trained on a diverse set of exploration policies. To overcome this limitation, we propose using the wrapped evaluation loss, which takes into account the model's consistency and is therefore sensitive to the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

The use of the wrapped evaluation loss leads to the development of a new algorithm, the sample-efficient maximum entropy policy synthesis estimator (SAMSE), which is shown to be superior to existing methods in complex environments requiring complex observations and multiple steps to complete a task.

Using advanced experimental techniques such as resonant x-ray diffraction and deep ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy, researchers have obtained new insights into the structures and electronic states of barium titanate and strontium titanate in their paraelectric phases. These findings reveal intricate titanate cage arrangements around alkaline earth metal ions and complex electronic distributions at the titanium atoms, offering a clear understanding of how these characteristics resist electric field-induced changes. This knowledge has been combined to create a theoretical framework that can predict the effects of structural changes on the electronic states in these materials. Utilizing this model, researchers were able to identify why certain experimental signals remain unresponsive to external influences, and it also facilitates the identification of potential phase transitions within these substances. This general approach can be applied to other similar materials, providing a valuable resource for researchers working with titanates. Due to the wide use of titanates in various applications and the significant impact of their properties on performance, this study yields significant outcomes. For instance, titanates are frequently employed as dynamic buffers in capacitors and as essential components in ferroelectric materials with memory functions. Furthermore, this research is relevant to the development of sensors capable of detecting subtle changes in the structure and chemistry of these materials. As a result, this study is a crucial step in the scientific exploration of these complex substances. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from two-dimensional images is a difficult task due to variations in lighting and the potential for additional shadows. This challenge is compounded by the presence of skin lesions, especially dark ones, which can significantly alter a face's appearance and create new shadows that interfere with model training. These issues are widespread and affect many individuals, making advanced 3D face reconstruction techniques that can account for such lesions a valuable contribution to the field. In response to these difficulties, we've developed a novel approach called SADRNet, which incorporates lesion areas into its models of the face, training on self-alignment and dual regression networks to produce more accurate and robust results. This approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, according to four key performance metrics, and the team behind SADRNet also provides a pre-trained model available for download. This model's capabilities were tested against a range of challenging scenarios, including face images with dark lesions, and the technical paper detailing these methods and tests has been submitted to CVPR 2021. This approach holds promise for a range of applications, from animation and video games to forensic science and biometric identification systems. This is particularly important in consideration of existing methods that either exclude individuals with dark lesions from their training datasets or devise specialized techniques tailored to specific individuals with light lesions. In contrast to these approaches, SADRNet's resilience to dark lesions makes it a more versatile and reliable solution for 3D face reconstruction tasks. This is further illustrated by a quantitative evaluation showing SADRNet's performance is consistently better than existing methods, even when tested against a subset of the training dataset. This finding is a key contribution of this research and has significant implications for the field. This is the first time a technical paper has presented a fully automatic 3D face reconstruction method capable of handling dark lesions, and the team behind this approach has open-sourced all necessary code and has made their model available for download. This framework is particularly useful for addressing errors and doubts in election ballot count outputs. We share a comprehensive dataset, along with a web-based tool for evaluating iOCR's performance. In recent years, understanding the behavior of models has become increasingly important, especially in linear models with time series data and over-parameterization. This paper focuses on a specific, under-explored scenario - benign misfitting - where there is no measurement error, no structural misspecification, and no colinearity. We investigate the performance of estimators, the behavior of optimization methods, and the properties of post-selection procedures in the absence of measurement error. Notably, we find that over-parameterization allows for identification and estimation without issues of colinearity. In practice, this means that standard methods for optimization and estimation still perform well, and post-selection procedures can produce accurate results. Additionally, the paper examines the effects of over-parameterization, including the non-archimedean property, and explores opportunities for adaptation of estimators under structural misspecification. This research provides insight into the behavior of models with over-parameterization and encourages further study of time series data with over-parameterization. The findings are demonstrated through simulation studies and application to real-world data. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.08652.

Specifically, $SL$ equals $SV$ multiplied by the square of a volume-related factor, referred to as the spectral shift in volume. Recent studies on text-to-SQL have primarily focused on executing database queries generated through natural language, with semantic meaning. However, current semantic parsers are limited to working within the same domain as the training data. This project aims to break this limitation by proposing a new, end-to-end parsing method that can translate natural language into SQL code across different domains. This new approach is a recursive neural network that generates database commands through single-round token mappings, allowing it to generalize beyond the same domain. Our proposed model executes database queries executed on multiple datasets, including Spider and SpiderCross, demonstrating superior performance when compared to baseline models. This new paradigm also produces enhanced token-level semantic meanings, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of text-to-SQL parsing. Furthermore, our model's ability to parse complex SQL syntax, combined with the generation of semantic meanings, marks a significant advancement in text-to-SQL parsing. This project's results suggest that a joint text-to-SQL parser can effectively capture both syntax and semantics within a database, even when the training and testing datasets are from different domains. This finding holds significant implications for the development of more adaptable and generalizable text-to-SQL parsers. This project's success also raises the question of what aspects of a database that the parser is aware of are domain-specific versus domain-agnostic. This awareness of the parser's capabilities will be crucial in guiding future work on cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing. In this research, we develop an automatic method for generating complex road networks to evaluate the performance of action-level keyframe synthesis techniques. Our approach builds upon B-spline curves to create challenging test scenarios, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through both theoretical analysis and practical evaluation of an existing ALKS algorithm. One significant advantage of our approach is the creation of infinite road network configurations, in contrast to previous methods that are limited to a single specific design. Additionally, our method enables the simulation of vehicle behavior within these generated environments, which is critical for assessing the realism of synthesized keyframes. To further validate our evaluation tool, we collected a dataset comprising human preferences for various road network configurations. Our findings indicate that optimizing an ALKS algorithm's performance solely based on accuracy can result in poorly performing models, highlighting the importance of incorporating diversity metrics in evaluation and suggesting several potential research directions for future exploration. Our evaluation dataset, consisting of challenging road network scenarios and corresponding human preference labels, is made available for the broader community to facilitate advancements in the field of action-level keyframe synthesis. This dataset complements existing collections of human-labeled data used to assess the efficacy of an ALKS algorithm, which employs deep learning-based models trained on massive datasets to generate realistic and engaging action sequences from video clips. Our evaluation framework consists of two components: a method for automatically generating diverse and challenging road network configurations, and a dataset of human preference labels for these test scenarios. Our results demonstrate the importance of considering both efficiency and effectiveness when evaluating the performance of ALKS algorithms, and we propose several potential extensions to further explore the capabilities of these algorithms for synthesizing complex action sequences from video clips. These melody captions aim to concisely summarize the primary melody present in each track, thereby providing listeners with a clearer understanding of the musical content. The findings indicate that incorporating these melody descriptions enhances user enjoyment and discovery experience when exploring music playlists. Temporal activity detection, a subtask of video analysis, involves identifying time intervals where actions occur. A key challenge lies in existing methods that often rely on predetermined features and boundaries, rather than learning context from the entire video. To address this, this paper proposes a novel framework, DCAN, which uses a dual context consolidation module to extract relevant information from two time windows surrounding a potential activity period. By incorporating this context through nonlinear interactions, DCAN enhances model performance on the Charades-ActANTion (C-A) dataset, achieving a mean average precision of 0.079, a significant improvement over existing methods. Experimental evaluations also demonstrate DCAN's effectiveness in accurately identifying activity start and end times. To facilitate model selection and error analysis, this paper introduces the use of a score function based on precision at different thresholds. Additionally, an open-source code for DCAN is made available online. Analyzing DCAN in more detail, the paper explores the effects of context size and number of layers, finding that these factors influence model performance but ultimately, a well-designed basic model yields optimal results. Further improvements to the state-of-the-art on C-A are also reported, with the best-rated method consisting of DCAN with two layers and a context size of 32, outperforming all competitors by a substantial margin of 0.058. 
This improved model is used in conjunction with a publicly accessible code at https://github.com/ikostadinov/DCAN, establishing a new golden standard for the field. Lastly, it is essential to note that DCAN is not a method for segmenting actions from raw video but rather a highly effective framework for determining time intervals where actions occur, based on the assumption that action segments are bounded and denoted on a scale from 0 to 1. This paper introduces the Bounded Action Video Dataset (BAVD), a new collection of action video datasets, comprising 17 classes with 1,014 annotated segments, and establishes a new baseline for temporal activity detection, outperforming all competitors by a significant margin of 0.058. 
In contrast to segmentation methods based on mask propagation and optical flow, BAVD focuses on bound detection, and all existing state-of-the-art methods on the Charades-ActANTion dataset are reconfirmed as top performers in this domain. Lastly, the paper explores the effects of bound detection and confirms its distinctiveness, as well as analyzing the differences between action video segmentation and bound detection, ultimately concluding that these are two distinct, separate problems. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic, with their precise origin unknown. This work seeks to shed light on this topic by presenting new analysis of previously collected data, along with fresh observations. A distinct connection between PTMs and the resulting changes in plasma edge localization has been discovered, which may be linked to the formation of an edge mode with a high frequency. Additionally, the relationship between electron heating and the rotation curve of the plasma has been explored, revealing that PTMs can cause localized increases in electron temperature that may result in enhanced edge plasma conductivity, leading to the localization of plasma edge currents. A connection between the localization of plasma edge currents and the formation of ITG-like instabilities has also been proposed. Furthermore, the proposed link between the localization of plasma edge currents and the localization of ITG-like instabilities has been supported by fresh data, showcasing the relevance of the edge electron temperature and the rotation curve in understanding this phenomenon. A proposed path for future research includes the examination of edge electron temperature and the rotation curve in other experiments. If the connection between the localization of plasma edge currents and the localization of ITG-like instabilities is validated in future research, it has the potential to contribute significantly to the broader understanding of edge localizations and mode formation in magnetic confinement devices. Additionally, the discovery of a link between the localization of plasma edge currents and the localization of ITG-like instabilities may also provide a pathway for the development of robust edge local stabilization methods, thus further exploring this understanding will be crucial for the advancement of future devices.

A common feature among materials that exhibit shear-induced softening or peakiness is the presence of multiple scale-dependent modes, which can be understood through a singular perturbation analysis near the primary transition at zero wavelength. This study investigates the behavior of these modes at longer wavelengths and confirms that they follow a universal scaling law related to the primary transition, for both elastic and glassy regimes. A new theoretical framework based on the concept of shear augmentation transitions is introduced, and it accurately predicts the modes' scaling laws across various materials with distinct elastic and plastic properties. This framework also enables the generation of scaled maps, which display a consistent structure that is independent of specific material properties. These findings provide a foundation for further exploring the underlying mechanics and dynamics of shear-induced phenomena and for developing a more general theory of shear states. The concept of localized shocks in conformal field theories, particularly in AdS$_5$, can be complicated by a collision of two closely spaced and parallel shocks. This paper seeks to analyze this scenario through a sequence of expanding shocks. By considering a sequence of shrinking domains of dependence, we can use the Bessel function expansion method, which effectively uses sequence expansions to capture localized behavior, to derive a general formula for the local operator displacement. This approach yields an asymptotic series, which can be interpreted as a sum of local contributions along the direction of shock movement and a super-deterministic sequence that encodes the inter-shock region's behavior. As the inter-shock distance decreases, the super-deterministic sequence plays a crucial role in determining whether the local operator displacement increases, decreases, or remains unchanged. This research builds upon prior work by the authors, which demonstrated that a certain Bessel function expansion met the requirements for the first shock, but encountered issues with convergence. The current study shows that the challenges associated with the second shock arise from a more intricate sequence of expansions, which involves multiple crossover events as the inter-shock distance decreases. The results obtained support the findings of Wilson-Fisher theory at the tricritical point, which indicates a more complex sequence of crossover events in AdS$_4$. The issue of convergence in AdS$_4$ suggests that the Bessel function expansion method may require a more sophisticated framework that accounts for infinite-order crossover phenomena. The proposed method can be applied to examine other shock collisions, such as transverse or frontal shocks, which could provide valuable insights into the behavior of boundary-less shocks and their interactions with each other and with walls. The research raises fundamental questions about the nature of local field theory and the significance of shock sequences, which may be related to the concept of sequences in physics. The study of sequence expansions in physics, which is an area that has been largely overlooked, may hold the key to addressing these questions and revealing the underlying structure of local field theory. When analyzing data from random processes, determining the most relevant parameters and discarding unnecessary ones is a complex challenge. This study addresses this issue by evaluating existing methods used to assess the importance of parameters in discrete data sets. Twenty-four different approaches were tested on simulated data sets with varying sample sizes, noise levels, and time series lengths. The results showed that only a few methods consistently produced reliable rankings of parameter importance, with the majority either failing to produce expected outcomes or producing inconsistent results. These exceptional methods included four that yielded accurate findings for all tested scenarios and one that achieved this consistency only with larger data sets. These findings highlight the necessity of rigorously testing any proposed method and the challenge of identifying suitable approaches for analyzing discrete data sets, especially those with short time frames. The study also provides specific guidance for choosing effective methods, emphasizing the importance of considering the underlying characteristics of the process being studied and ensuring that any assessment technique is robust and consistent across different data sets. The research concludes by highlighting the value of further developing alternative, more efficient methods for evaluating parameter importance. The emergence of Edge Computing is driven by the need for faster, more reliable, and less expensive data processing. To cater to this shift, Edge Solutions are being developed to support a variety of critical applications, including those with significant implications for society, security, and the economy, such as medical diagnosis, financial transactions, and electoral systems. Unfortunately, many Edge Solutions are being deployed without thorough security testing, largely due to limited resources and a lack of effective, event-focused security testing methods suitable for Edge Environments. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel testing framework called EFT-EC, designed to guide developers in creating secure Edge Solutions through a focused approach on critical events. By leveraging this framework, developers can pinpoint sensitive events within their code and generate targeted, high-priority tests, leading to more efficient and effective security testing. Additionally, the paper reports on a case study involving the development of an event-driven secure testing tool, as well as a survey examining the current state of secure testing in the Edge Computing community. With the rapid growth of Edge Computing, the introduction of EFT-EC is an important step forward, offering a practical solution for secure testing that can inspire further innovation and collaboration. The development of advanced autonomous vehicle navigation systems requires substantial progress in generating realistic traffic scenarios. Current methods for scenario creation, whether using graph-based models or 3D point clouds, fall short in producing scenarios that accurately mirror actual driving environments. These deficiencies stem from an overreliance on manually crafted graphs and 3D models that are either too primitive or too derived from real-world scenes, neglecting the expertise of experienced scenario leaders who have spent countless hours fine-tuning these scenarios. To tackle this challenge, we propose SceneGen, a novel approach to scenario creation that leverages the guidance of human experts through interactive mapping, thus enabling the generation of highly realistic and diverse scenarios. By testing SceneGen on the NuScenes dataset, we demonstrate its capacity to create scenarios that are not only visually comparable to real scenes but also accurately assessed by human evaluators. Furthermore, SceneGen showcases its efficiency in producing multiple scenario iterations and validates the crucial role of human guidance in the scenario creation process. The project's code and evaluations are publicly available at https://github.com/waymo-research/Scenegen. Additionally, we invite other researchers to collaborate with us on this project. One of the competition tracks allows participants to build upon SceneGen using a publicly accessible repository. A control system is designed to adjust the position of the LDV system in real-time, based on the measured velocities. This control system is tested with two different configurations, and the resulting two-dimensional velocity fields are compared to actual measurements made with a fully functional 2D LDV system, foraging. The findings show that single-point LDV systems, even when distantly controlled, can effectively obtain two-dimensional velocity data. This research is particularly relevant to situations where fully functional 2D LDV systems cannot be employed due to the large distance between the LDV system and the measurement area, often a constraint in large-scale applications. As a case study, the paper explores its application in measuring velocity fields in oceanic flows, specifically in monitoring coastal oceanic flows off the beach, a critical area that has been the subject of previous LDV experiments. The data obtained with the distant-controlled single-point LDV system, with a control system developed in this study, is compared to that obtained with the fully functional 2D LDV system, for a flow depth of 0.305m. One lesser explored aspect is the encoding of participant information, which we argue is crucial for a realistic social context. In this paper, we raise the question of whether these models' encoder representations adequately capture the identity of the speaker. We design various tests to evaluate this, including verifying that these representations aren't simply relying on easy-to-extract features from the input, and that they're sensitive to changes in the speaker's intent. Our results indicate that these tests pose a significant challenge for the current generation of conversation models, which we attribute to the limited size of the datasets used to train them. Ultimately, we find that a model which is trained to retain more information in the encoder representations, using a speaker-aware protocol, not only performs better in the tests but also exhibits better coherence in the generated responses. Additionally, our results demonstrate that these models are naturally multi-task capable, as the protocol used during training influences the generated responses. In order to maintain the test's ground truth, we made the decision to maintain the current evaluation protocol but test the model with a different name. In conclusion, our research indicates that the current generation of conversation models falls short of mimicking the way humans retain information about social interactions. We employ the finite-temperature response function technique to examine the heating effects of a point charge in doped graphene, considering both the absence and presence of a ground state described by the Dirac-Fermi-Sea. At sub-lattice temperatures, the thermal influence is noticeable in the electronic density distribution around the point charge; we quantify this impact as the finite-temperature shielding exponent. This paper introduces a novel computational approach for determining the maximum reachable area around a mobile robot within a specified time frame, subject to certain control limitations. Unlike traditional methods which rely on dynamic programming but are hindered by the inability to solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation explicitly, our proposal utilizes a reformulated variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation and leverages its semi-explicit solution to calculate the attainable set. Specifically, we first reformulate the problem as solving a certain type of variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation with an initial condition, and then propose a numerical solution using an explicit representation of the value function, which enables the computation of the attainable set via a system of semi-implicit Hamilton-Jacobi equations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method for computing the reachable set for a mobile robot subject to state-dependent control inputs on a 2D domain. Unlike existing methods which assume a specific control policy, our proposal can handle a more general set of control options, and we show that our method can produce more accurate results compared to existing approaches which assume a simpler control strategy. We examine the spatial dimensions of young stellar associations in six nearby galaxies using infrared color-magnitude diagrams, and compare their distribution in mass-adapted bins. A comprehensive study of $10,000$ young stellar objects in these galaxies reveals a average scale of $10^2$ parsecs for their projected distances, with a scatter of one order of magnitude. The dimensions of these associations are unaffected by the mass of the stars within them. Our analysis also shows that the associations break into smaller groups at higher mass levels, above $8M_\odot$. These results challenge the widely accepted idea that all low-mass stars in these associations form in a single collapse. Instead, multiple small-scale collapses are favored. Additionally, the diminished sizes of these associations among more massive stars may indicate a shorter disk accretion phase or faster cooling and collapse. 

Finally, considering the proportions of these stars in our sample, we find that the dimensions of these associations are similar to those of the Orion Nebula star-forming region, and that the star formation efficiency of these associations remains constant across the six galaxies studied here. 

The detailed data presented here will enable further comparison with theoretical models of star formation, while the results obtained from our analysis are presented in the figures and discussion sections of this paper. 

In the appendix, we outline the methodology used for correcting the observations and identifying the young stellar objects in this study. 

The dimensions of these associations are investigated further in Figure 5 of the supplementary material, which displays the average size of the associations at different mass levels in the six galaxies studied here.

Some general principles and specific examples and counterexamples are explored and discussed. Some open questions are also raised. 

Firstly, when $L$ is mapped to its image under an expansion or contraction homomorphism for a free group of the same rank, the resulting topological entropy or shift complexity will be the original value multiplied by the rank of the free group. If the rank is increased from $N$ to $M$, the new entropy or complexity will be the original value times the greater of $N$ and $M$. If the rank is decreased from $N$ to $M$, the new entropy or complexity will be the original value times the greater of $N$ and $M$, unless the original shift has full topological entropy when considered as a subshift over $F_N$, in which case it is equal to $N$. When the underlying free group basis is changed from $F_N$ to $F_M$, with $N$ not equal to $M$, the resulting topological entropy or shift complexity will be equal to the larger of $N$ and $M$. Some specific examples and counterexamples are provided for these scenarios. 

If $L$ is a free group generated by a non-empty finite set of reduced words over $F_N$, with rank $N$ greater than one, the topological entropy or shift complexity for its factor shifts will be zero. If $L$ is equal to the entire free group over $F_N$, with rank $N$ greater than one, the topological entropy or shift complexity for its factor shifts will be equal to $N$. 

Some open questions are also raised in this paper, specifically regarding the relationship between topological entropy, shift complexity and recognition of free groups, as well as the behavior of these quantities when the underlying free group basis is changed from $F_N$ to $F_M$, with $N$ not equal to $M$. Additionally, the paper raises the question of whether there are any naturally occurring subshifts that could be isomorphic to free groups over $F_N$, with $N$ greater than one.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization abilities of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-enhanced approach called multiple-round self-evaluation, which allows models to compare their generated outputs with a diverse range of competing predictions.
This evaluation helps the model identify and produce more accurate and semantically rich responses in an unsupervised context, where the evaluation results are used to refine its output through a contrastive loss function.
We apply this approach to 12 diverse text-to-text tasks and find that it significantly improves performance, achieving an average gain of 4.5 points in the F1 score or $0.23$ in the meteoric score.
Notably, some models exhibit over-specialization in certain tasks, but our proposed method effectively mitigates this issue, leading to a more consistent 10% gain across all evaluated tasks.

The theory of Generalized Expectancy suggests that drug use is influenced by a person's overall worldview, comprised of five fundamental components: locus of control, future time perspective, self concept, responsibility, and hardiness. Previous studies have demonstrated a positive correlation between these cognitive characteristics and a person's likelihood to engage in drug use, with the strongest associations found for self concept and locus of control. However, the scope of these relationships has yet to be comprehensively understood. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of assessing drug use risk through these five dimensions. A statistical analysis of over 1,600 urine samples collected from individuals on probation, alongside their self-reported assessments on the GEQ-SF5 questionnaire, revealed a significant positive correlation between the scores indicating a harder individual's reduced likelihood of drug use. Conversely, higher self concept scores were associated with increased drug use, defying the initial hypothesis. Models predicting drug use based on the five-factor model showed a moderate level of accuracy, with the hardest and lowest self concept individuals exhibiting the greatest difference in predicted drug use probabilities. These findings suggest that assessing an individual's drug use risk through the five-factor model can be a useful approach, with implications for developing more effective and personalized treatment plans.

We present ATOMIC, a knowledge atlas designed to enable the evaluation of machine common knowledge through rule-based inference. This atlas constitutes a diverse catalog of statements comprising 399 implicit rules derived from 157 distinct sets of facts, drawn from a diverse range of sources. These implicit rules can be utilized to assess a machine's ability to perform inductive reasoning, deducing new facts based on previously established ones. Additionally, we introduce CausalCOP, a novel game aimed at testing a machine's capacity to understand causal relationships and its extension to multiple languages through natural language prompts. Furthermore, we introduce several challenges and benchmarks for inductive machine common knowledge as well as protocols for evaluation through human-generated data and scoring via human-in-the-loop methods. ATOMIC's knowledge atlas and associated challenges are made publicly accessible at https://atomic.evi.com. We also introduce CausalCOP, a test suite for a machine's understanding of causal relationships, and our code is available at https://causalcop.evi.com. Both initiatives provide a foundation for exploring the development of machines equipped with fundamental knowledge and reasoning capabilities. As part of the CausalCOP release, we include a prototype for a machine learning model named CausalCOP-M, whose performance we assess against the standards set by the challenges and benchmarks defined within the ATOMIC atlas. CausalCOP-M is an example of a machine that has been trained on a diverse dataset but fails to meet the requirements for inductive machine common knowledge as outlined in the challenges and benchmarks. Moreover, we introduce HumanCOP, a human-level counterpart to CausalCOP-M, demonstrating human performance on the same test suite and finding that certain aspects of human cognition are inherently difficult to model with machine learning. This distinction is particularly notable as HumanCOP's abilities and limitations mirror the standards set by the challenges and benchmarks within the ATOMIC atlas. We anticipate that both ATOMIC and CausalCOP will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of machines equipped with fundamental knowledge and reasoning capabilities and will provide a framework for evaluating the progress made in this area. As machine learning models become increasingly sophisticated, it is essential to ensure that they are also capable of understanding basic causal relationships and the implicit connections that exist throughout human common knowledge. To enhance data efficiency of end-to-end ASR models, they can be trained with text data, allowing the model to learn from both speech and text information. This multi-modal setup enables the model to leverage the knowledge embedded in large text datasets, facilitating low-resource speech recognition tasks. This paper proposes a bidirectional focused attention mechanism that allows the model to learn from and make use of both speech and text data during training. This two-way attention mechanism differs from previous single-modal attention mechanisms, allows the model to learn more effective representations, and results in performance improvements on both zero-shot and few-shot speech recognition tasks. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech dataset reveal a 4.5% relative improvement in subword ASR accuracy in a zero-shot setting and a 11.4% relative improvement in a few-shot setting. Additionally, our proposed model achieves comparable performance to model fine-tuned on only speech data with a 25 times reduction in training data. This efficiency is attributed to a 73% reduction in training data without additional hyperparameter tuning. These gains come with no additional computational costs during inference. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/seyed-gh/bidirectional-multi-modal. This multi-modal setup with our proposed bidirectional focused attention mechanism has the potential to revolutionize end-to-end ASR systems by enabling them to generalize well to unseen data. This is particularly relevant in the context of transfer learning and domain adaptation, where the ability to generalize well is crucial. Our proposed approach can be viewed as a form of transfer learning that allows the model to leverage the knowledge embedded in text data during speech recognition tasks. This multi-modal setup with our proposed bidirectional focused attention mechanism has the potential to enhance the performance of other related systems that generalize well to unseen data. Initial conditions for relativistic hydrodynamic descriptions of the quark-gluon plasma in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions can be linked to final-state particle distributions. This connection allows for the interpretation of in-medium processes like jet fragmentation and medium response in terms of inelastic scattering. We show that the inelastic cross section for jet fragments to scatter off the quark-gluon plasma is large, approximately in the range of $10-100 \, \mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$, which implies a significant reduction in jet energy due to scattering. The associated energy transfer to the medium, however, is highly dispersed and unlikely to result in the formation of particles carrying a significant fraction of their four-momentum. These findings suggest that particles carrying a large fraction of the momentum of a scattered jet fragment are likely to originate from additional scattering or intermediate meson decays rather than the primary scattering event. These results also highlight the limitations of traditional jet quenching models that assume a fixed scattering length and emphasize the importance of accounting for transverse momentum transfers within the quark-gluon plasma when interpreting data from jet quenching. Furthermore, we identify potential signatures for detecting scattering at intermediate scales, which could provide insight into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. These signatures include the distribution of particles carrying a large fraction of the momentum of a scattered jet fragment, which could be explored through an event-by-event analysis of jet fragments using Monte Carlo simulations of heavy-ion collisions with coupled hydrodynamics and jet energy deposition. This could offer a more nuanced understanding of jet quenching and the behavior of the quark-gluon plasma within ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions. Predicting future video frames from a sequence of past observations is a complex task, especially when there are significant delays between these events. This challenge is exemplified by the task of perspective video forecasting, which involves determining the position and movements of individuals within a scene from a first-person observer. This study presents an innovative approach to this challenge, combining a dual representation of the observer and surrounding environment to inform future state predictions. This dual representation encompasses both the observer's visual field and their movement intentions, which are modeled through a pose graph. This pose graph is utilized to make predictions about the observer's position, movements, and surrounding environment, which are confirmed to be the most reliable features for this task. This representation's dual nature enables robust predictions, even when the observer is occluded, and facilitates seamless extension to multi-person scenarios. This study also introduces a challenging dataset and evaluation protocols tailored to perspective video forecasting, which underscores the difficulty of developing general prediction models for this task. Our proposed approach demonstrates exceptional performance on this dataset in comparison to established baselines. This approach's effectiveness is further verified through the integration of a robust pose estimator, which yields optimal results. This study presents a novel solution for predicting the observer's movements and surrounding environment, which could also be applied to control the observer's movement in real-time. This approach's multi-person extension holds significant potential for collaborative applications. This study's challenging dataset and evaluation protocols serve as a benchmark for the development of public datasets for similar prediction tasks. This study also explores the integration of its model with real-time applications, which could be used to enhance the performance of sports analytics, surveillance systems, and robotic navigation. This study's results demonstrate the benefits of generalizing prediction models to account for temporal disparities, which is essential for real-world scenarios.
