Two essential approaches exist for estimating sea surface roughness, namely the Cox and Munk method and the ISASS technique. While ISASS has been the preferred method for use in radiance simulations due to its accuracy, it has limitations when it comes to spatial and temporal implementation. On the other hand, the Cox and Munk method is straightforward but tends to overestimate roughness. This study investigates the characteristics of wave crests rather than sea surface slopes in calculating roughness, based on infrared radiance observations from space. Wave crests rather than individual surface elements are responsible for contributing to the total radiance, which provides a new perspective on ocean surface characterization. This approach demonstrates the ability to determine the distribution of wave crests without relying on slope probability functions, which are subject to bias. Consequently, this study finds that wave crests follow a Weibull distribution with a shape parameter of approximately 2.1, which is a key finding for future research on ocean surface characterization. This study also explores various parameters that describe wave crests, such as the ratio of wave crests to ocean autocorrelation length, which provides valuable information for future applications of wave crests in ocean remote sensing. Ultimately, this study offers a new perspective for characterizing ocean surfaces through wave crests, which could potentially replace traditional slope-based approaches. This approach is not only applicable to optical observations but also has implications for the design of future ocean color and thermal infrared missions. This approach is not exclusive to optical observations but is also relevant to the design of future thermal infrared missions that observe the ocean. Layer-by-layer conduction measurement techniques reveal unique conduction behaviors in different layers of materials, offering a chance to understand interlayer interactions and the possibility of hidden conduction pathways. However, these techniques require precise control of layer separation, which is challenging for cuprate superconductors with charge density waves. Here, we propose a mathematical framework and a numerical method to extract useful information from interlayer conduction measurements, even in the presence of charge density oscillations. By applying our approach to existing layer-by-layer measurement data of Tl-2201, a cuprate superconductor, we uncover evidence of enhanced conduction at particular layer separations, and identify an interlayer conduction tunneling barrier with a height of approximately 0.25 eV. Our model also considers the impact of charge density oscillations on conduction and suggests that superconducting correlations extend beyond nearest-neighbor layers. These findings provide a foundation for reinterpreting existing layer-by-layer measurement data and will facilitate future investigation of interlayer conduction in cuprate superconductors. Furthermore, our model is versatile and can be adapted to analyze conduction in other materials with layered structures. The code utilized in this research is available upon request. The maintenance of linear stability in roto-gravitational fields for rotating stars, particularly their bar-mode oscillations, relies on adiabatic indices along radial lines (meridians) and circular great circles. However, calculating adiabatic indices within meridians is complicated due to the irregular geometry, resulting in only approximate, model-specific values being available. In contrast, general relativity's hydrodynamical equations can be used to derive the adiabatic index along circular great circles for stars made of dense matter, without relying on the geometry of rotation. This approach yields an expression for the adiabatic index in terms of sound speed and the metric components under specific relativistic perfect fluid theories, including quark stars and hybrid stars, and we demonstrate that the index values obtained are consistent with those from relativistic stellar stability studies. Furthermore, we investigate the sound speed profiles necessary to maintain linear stability in these compact stars. In the case of meson-dominated cores, where hadrons are non-interacting, the index is consistent with the hadronic value. However, in the hadron sphere, especially when mesons do not disappear at the hadron boundary, the index requires a higher sound speed than in the meson domain to prevent bar-mode instability. Multi-encoder models that incorporate a grid of entrances allow a model to focus on specific local details within an input, however they pose a challenge because they are inherently unselective. This unselectivity leads to difficulties such as overfitting, needing multiple entrances, and a significant increase in model size. Our proposed module, a dynamic entrance layer, overcomes these challenges by selectively leveraging certain input elements. We implemented this layer within a grid-based encoder setup, known as the dynamic entrance grid (DIG), which achieved exceptional results in multiple experiments involving text-based classification tasks, significantly outperforming both standard transformers and the existing attention-based grid encoder models that promote selection. The DIG model also exhibits a notable advantage of having a significantly smaller model size compared to its grid encoder counterparts. The code for the proposed model has been made publicly available on GitHub at the time of submission. 

In more detail, our proposed module builds upon the global mean pooling layer by incorporating an affine transformation to refine the model's selection. We experiment with two variants of this layer: a soft variant with a small additional parameter count and a hard variant with no additional parameters, which allows the model to focus on the most representative elements of the input. When integrated into a grid encoder setup with multiple encoder layers, the soft variant led to state-of-the-art performance in the VQA v2 benchmark, achieving an accuracy of 48.1%. Furthermore, the proposed DIG model exhibits a significant advantage of having a much smaller model size compared to its grid encoder counterparts. 

The proposed module can be a useful alternative to traditional multi-head self-attention layers, especially in scenarios where the input data has a grid-like structure such as images and videos. Additionally, the proposed module is more efficient in terms of model size compared to attention-based grid encoder models.

This paper examines the impact of $\gamma$ variations on parallax determinations from Gaia-like astrometry, considering three possible scenarios for post-Newtonian effects: a static $\gamma$ value, a $\gamma$ value that varies with position, and a $\gamma$ value that changes over time. For a static $\gamma$ value, deviations in parallax estimations are linked to the product of post-Newtonian effects, mass, and distance, with a maximum error of 0.5 $\mu$as in the global solution. When $\gamma$ is allowed to fluctuate with position but remains constant over time, post-Newtonian effects on parallax determinations are significantly increased, with potential errors reaching 5-10 $\mu$s in the global solution. If $\gamma$ is assumed to change over time, corrections to parallax estimations become more complex and dependent on several factors, including mass, distance, and time. This added complexity may increase post-Newtonian effects on parallax determinations even further. It is essential to control for post-Newtonian effects when analyzing internal astrometry, especially for objects with low parallax angles, as they can distort findings and mask true variations in parallax. Furthermore, considering post-Newtonian effects is crucial for accurately determining mass values, particularly for massive objects like binary systems and globular clusters. In contrast, the impact of post-Newtonian effects on the mass-to-light ratio ratio is minimal, at less than 0.5%. Finally, the paper suggests that future Gaia data analysis should account for post-Newtonian effects on parallax estimations, employing a static $\gamma$ value as a first approximation and factoring in potential fluctuations in $\gamma$ to derive more accurate mass values. This is especially important for detecting subtle variations in parallax, as well as determining the mass-to-light ratio of open clusters and binary systems. This approach enables internal astrometry with reduced systematic effects and minimal contamination from binary systems, thus yielding more accurate mass values and mass-to-light ratios. In one-dimensional discrete quantum systems with short-range interactions, a new class of self-sustaining waves called self-boosted solitons exists. These waves maintain their form without external influences by receiving a continuous, low-intensity "boost" from nearby sites. This phenomenon occurs naturally at any speed within a system's overall bandwidth and can be understood through a representation that transforms the discrete system into a equivalent continuous one. This representation reveals the requirements necessary for a self-boosted soliton to exist and it shows that these solutions are topologically protected, meaning they are resistant to changes in system parameters. Self-boosted solitons can also be created and destroyed at specific locations within a system, providing a new mechanism for energy transfer over long distances. These waves have implications for the understanding of non-equilibrium systems and may provide a new way to manufacture and control discrete solitons.

Our solution, a new framework called SIMC 2.0, enables an ML model to be trained while protecting itself from malicious clients that may manipulate input data. We demonstrate SIMC 2.0's effectiveness by applying it to a popular ML model, but also identify its limitations. Additionally, we explore ways to enhance training efficiency and create a new, open-source training framework called R2D2, which combines the benefits of both secure and efficient training. R2D2's performance is comparable to that of an optimized, unsecured model, while providing full protection against malicious clients. We believe R2D2 may serve as a reference design for the development of future secure ML models. Our research and analysis are supported by thorough security and performance analyses, along with new security proofs and empirical evaluations. Furthermore, we introduce a new attack technique called the "low-high injection attack" and validate the efficiency of R2D2 through practical experiments. On the other hand, we discover that SIMC 2.0 may fail to protect against highly sophisticated malicious clients and identify key limitations in current cryptographic techniques that could further enhance the security of ML models. Our research also raises new challenges for the development of secure ML models and could potentially inspire the creation of new, more secure models. The spiral galaxy M101, located approximately 20 million light-years from Earth, has been extensively studied with radio telescopes. A recent 319 MHz bandwidth observation of M101 with the FAST radio telescope revealed the detection of multiple high-velocity HI clouds beyond the galaxy's outer limits, as well as a newly discovered HI tail on M101's side opposite to the direction of the galaxy Abell 2415. The abundance of extragalactic HI clouds in this observation poses a low detection rate, around 10%, which is consistent with predictions from the VIRGO-Hi gas field simulations. The mass of the M101 galaxy group is estimated to be approximately 2.1 x 10^11 solar masses, and the group's gas fraction is found to be 0.04, which is a fractionally low value compared to other galaxy groups of similar mass. The detection of the HI tail in M101 suggests a past galaxy merger, which may have contributed to the formation of the massive stellar ring observed around M101. The ring's age is estimated to be around 1.2 billion years, which is significantly younger than the galaxy's other features. The ring's age determines its break-up time, which is now in the past, and as a result, the ring is no longer visible in optical light due to being dissipated by M101's gravitational field. The interaction between M101 and Abell 2415 is occurring at a highly oblique angle, which may contribute to the detection of the HI tail and surrounding clouds. The group's major axis is structured by M101's central spiral arms and a newly discovered small spiral galaxy, NGC 4605D. The detection of the HI tail and surrounding clouds in M101 adds it to the exclusive list of galaxies that have experienced tidal interactions and breaks, along with IC 1101, IC 1755, and NGC 4507. The unique features of the M101 galaxy group make it an ideal subject for further radio telescope observations. The large beam size of the FAST radio telescope allows it to make such detections possible, and the uniqueness of its observations opens up the possibility of making similar discoveries with other radio telescopes. The possible presence of HI clouds and a tail in the M101 galaxy group were first revealed by recent radio telescope observations, and further research is needed to better understand the true extent and characteristics of these features, as well as the history and dynamics of the M101 galaxy group. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, a current issue in machine reading comprehension arises. Existing approaches typically rely on superficial features and may not fully capture the underlying semantics of the question. To address this limitation, we propose a semantic-aware multi-facet framework that not only considers the question's surface-level features but also a distributional representation of the question's semantics. This distributional representation is obtained through a contextualized embedding method, enabling the model to capture implicit relationships and a semantic hierarchy among entities. By incorporating this distributional representation, the model's performance is significantly enhanced on the CommonsenseQA dataset, a leading benchmark in this domain. Specifically, our baseline model achieves a 36.4% gap in performance when compared to a state-of-the-art strong baseline, demonstrating the effectiveness of our semantic-aware approach. Furthermore, our model's ability to generalize is demonstrated through the discovery of novel semantic connections between entities, providing a promising direction for future work. 

In addition to semantic-aware multi-facet reasoning, our framework is well-suited for addressing the issue of data imbalance in datasets, such as CommonsenseQA. By incorporating a careful sampling method, we are able to reduce the significant performance gap observed in previously proposed solutions. For example, on the CommonsenseQA dataset, our method is able to achieve a 12.6% gap in performance improvement when compared to the strongest competing approach. We believe our framework is generally applicable and is thus evaluated on multiple open-domain question answering datasets, including CommonsenseQA, CommonsenseQA (augmented), Commonsense Catalyst, and Commonsense Catalyst (augmented). The code and distributional representations for the question semantics are available for download at https://github.com/zheng-wei-liu/coarse-to-careful.

The judicious co-administration of medications represents a complex challenge, largely stemming from the intricate relationships between drugs and their targets, as well as limited clinical information available to healthcare professionals. A key obstacle lies in healthcare professionals' difficulty in navigating vast amounts of clinical data, including outdated knowledge and outdated regulations, which they must consider when evaluating medications. A significant source of this difficulty stems from the absence of a unified framework for integrating multi-faceted information about medications, targets, and adverse effects. A further complication arises from the varying nature of data, including both structured and unstructured forms, which presents a unified representation challenge. To address these challenges, researchers have begun exploring deep learning techniques that prioritize connections and relationships. This survey paper offers a comprehensive exploration of these deep learning methods from a unified perspective, discussing models of graph convolution, based on shared representations, as well as other forms, such as sequence-to-sequence and attention-based models. It also delves into the use of combination models and specialized architectures for target prediction. Furthermore, it discusses applications of these methods in medication pairs, including both individual drugs, as well as co-administered medications, and covers evaluation protocols, performance benchmarks, and real-world deployment. This survey also discusses open issues, such as the development of more robust evaluation protocols, as well as the creation of more accessible and reliable deep learning-based target prediction tools. This includes challenges related to model interpretability, the incorporation of domain knowledge, and the design of more effective adversarial training methods. This survey is targeted at both healthcare professionals and AI/ML researchers, with the goal of advancing the field of deep learning for medication pairs. This includes both individual drugs and co-administered medications, as well as target prediction more broadly. This paper introduces a novel approach, Federated Learning from Diversified Walks (FLDW), which leverages random strolls of students to enhance teacher learning on a diverse dataset. FLDW addresses several challenges faced by existing federated learning frameworks, including the limited quality of student updates, the high communication cost, and the risk of data leakage. By incorporating random strolls, FLDW procures a affordable and high-quality training experience for students, enabling them to engage in frequent updates with the teacher. We evaluate FLDW through FLDW Walks and a modified Split-Batch strategy, both of which demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency in training models from datasets with diverse samples. Our experiments showcase the versatility of FLDW, applying it to the training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for both image and text classification tasks. The results show substantial improvements over traditional federated learning and other baseline strategies. Our code is publicly available on the Learning Dynamics repository. Research indicates a link between mental illness and higher recidivism rates. This study examines the effect on psychological well-being of mandating therapy for offenders. Despite initial improvements, participants in the mandated therapy group eventually showed similar self-reported mental health outcomes as a comparison group that received usual care in prison. Interestingly, the mandated therapy group exhibited a higher rate of rearrest within two years of release from prison. These findings suggest that compulsory therapy may have an unintended consequence of reducing psychological well-being in the short term and increasing the likelihood of reoffending in the long term. Several potential explanations for these outcomes are explored. This research is an initial examination of a larger randomized controlled trial of psychological therapy for offenders and future studies will investigate the effect of different types of therapy. Despite significant advancements in image segmentation using deep learning models, the challenge remains when it comes to semi-supervised pixel-level classification. The issue lies in effectively utilizing a large quantity of unlabeled data to improve model performance with a limited number of annotated images. To tackle this problem, various regularization techniques have been developed to constrain model outputs on unlabeled data, thus preventing overfitting and enabling the extraction of meaningful features from abundant image data. These techniques include adversarial training, metadata preservation, cross-domain translation, and more, though many of these methods are complex and difficult to optimize. In contrast, a straightforward regularization technique is proposed, based on simply ensuring that the output probabilities of the model, when applied to unlabeled data, adhere to the definition of probability measures. This technique leverages unlabeled data to constrain the model's output distributions, promoting a more coherent representation of image contents. The proposed method is evaluated on the Cambridge Land Cover Dataset and the ISIC 2019 Melanoma Atlas, demonstrating its efficacy in enhancing model performance with a vast amount of unlabeled data. Results indicate significant improvements in classification accuracy with the proposed technique, outperforming existing methods in some cases. Furthermore, the technique exhibits a simple and flexible design, facilitating easy integration with deep learning models. The ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system, relying on the decision of which events to process further, utilizes a multi-level system for real-time analysis. This study presents the design of a new, high-performance electronics board called the "Type-B" board, designed for the second level of this process. Developed using an Advanced Telecommunications Computing Architecture (ATCA) blade as a base, this Type-B board features 6 high-speed transceivers for data communication and 2 Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) known as the "Type-A" Front End Board interfaces. With a data transfer rate of 1.6 gigabytes per second, this Type-B board will be paired with the Type-A board to form a complete system. Currently in the prototype testing phase, these Type-B boards are set to be mass-produced using an "Ultrascale+" technology to replace the existing, less performant boards. The development of this Type-B board utilized a hybrid approach of in-house design and collaboration with external companies. The performance of this new board, exceeding the requirements set for it, is expected to significantly improve the detection capabilities of the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider when incorporated into the jet calorimeter trigger system. The decision time for processing events with this new system will be approximately half that of the current technology. The development of this Type-B board has demonstrated the feasibility of using "Ultrascale+" technology in the ATLAS experiment and potential future applications. In 1928, Lewis proposed the Ziegler-Lewi (ZL) criterion to predict polarisation probabilities in atoms. We've developed a novel graph neural network called the Ziegler-Lewi model, which accurately predicts angular and linear photoionisation probabilities in nitrogens and oxygen's ground states under circular polarised light. Our approach uses an intuitive graph that represents an atom's electronic configuration and accurately captures the effects of spin interactions. By providing clear visual representations of electron relationships, this model surpasses previous methods in interpretability, enabling a deeper understanding of the complex processes involved in its predictions. Our research demonstrates the potential for graph neural networks to make significant contributions to the study of atomic physics. Additionally, we've released a publicly accessible repository containing our model's code and associated data, which can serve as a benchmark for further advancements in this field. Our findings also suggest opportunities for applications in related areas, such as molecular physics and quantum chemistry. Our analysis of our model's predictions identified patterns that could be interpreted as manifestations of chaotic behavior in atomic systems, characterised by the sudden onset of stability in regions of high probability, and the emergence of periodic patterns following a transition. These patterns hold the potential to be exploited in future studies of quantum chaos. Our approach has also enabled the creation of visual representations of electron states that could be used in the development of educational virtual labs and interactive simulations. By combining artificial intelligence with educational tools, we have created an interactive visualization tool that allows users to explore and experience the unique state transitions in our model, including the patterns associated with chaotic behavior, and we have incorporated it into our publicly accessible repository. Our research has been supported by the University of Adelaide's Institute for Intelligent Systems and the Australian Research Council. We have also received funding from the University of Adelaide's Faculty of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences. Additionally, we have collaborated with the University of Adelaide's Centre for Artificial Intelligence. We have used our model to investigate the effects of different light polarisation on the ionisation of nitrogen and oxygen, and our findings have been presented at the 2019 Australian Institute of Physics Congress and the 2020 Neural Information Processing Systems Conference, and are scheduled for presentation at the 2023 International Conference on Machine Learning. Our work has been recognized with the 2020 University of Adelaide Three Minute Thesis Competition's People's Choice award and the 2021 Neural Information Processing Systems Conference's Best Application and System Paper award. We have also received the 2022 University of Adelaide Alumni Award for Early Career Researchers

To evaluate and compare such embedding methods, a diverse range of benchmark datasets is essential. This paper introduces Twitch Players, a newly created dataset derived from the Twitch gaming network, consisting of 10,534 players organized into 2,518 teams by their proximity and structural roles. Additionally, 500 opposing pairs are identified and used to evaluate the ability of proximity and role-based node embeddings to distinguish between them. The evaluation results show that both types of node embeddings can effectively capture some aspect of a player's proximity and structural role within their team, but they can also be easily tricked by players from opposing teams who share similar network positions. To facilitate further comparison and validation of node embeddings, Twitch Players is made available for public use. To validate the uniqueness of this dataset, a statistical analysis is conducted to assure that it represents an authentic reflection of the underlying network characteristics. Finally, the dataset's potential extensions and potential applications in areas like social network analysis and machine learning are also explored. Furthermore, the paper is open to feedback and suggestions from the research community. This paper presents a novel approach to achieving accurate force control in series elastic actuators (SEAs). SEAs are renowned for their ability to efficiently absorb shocks and minimize the risk of actuator overload. However, accurately estimating the stiffness of their elastic elements in order to precisely calculate the transmission factor has proven to be a challenging problem. As a result, the high degree of uncertainty associated with SEA transmission factors hinders their effective use in applications requiring precise force regulation. To address this issue, a robust and straightforward transmission force observer was developed, which utilizes a minimal number of sensory feedback measurements to estimate the elastic element's force displacement. By providing an accurate estimation of the force transmission factor, this observer enables SEA's actual force transmission behavior to match its designed specification. In order to evaluate the performance of this novel observer, a specifically designed SEA test bed was constructed and a robust control system was implemented using a simple feedback controller. The results obtained with the proposed observer were compared to those of a regular SEA that relies on a default transmission factor and the former's performance was found to be more precise. The improvement in performance was consistently observed across multiple tests conducted under different stiffness settings. As a conclusion, the paper's novel transmission force observer provides a feasible solution to the challenge of precise force regulation in SEAs and it has been successfully validated through actual hardware tests. This solution is particularly appealing as it is both uncomplicated and robust. Furthermore, the paper's findings are also applicable to other similar types of elastic actuators. To ensure the safety of underwater robots, predicting the movements of marine animals is crucial. Underwater robots must anticipate and adapt to the changing swimming patterns of these animals as they navigate through the water. By assuming the water remains calm and undisturbed, we can apply Gaussian Process regression to forecast the animals' position based on their past swimming patterns. However, this approach fails to account for the possibility of water turbulence affecting the animals' movement. To address this limitation, we enhance Gaussian Process regression with additional factors such as the animals' speed and orientation in the water. By modeling these factors as stationary processes that vary over time, we can combine them with the original Gaussian Process model. This integrated model allows the estimation of a covariance function for the animals' movement, taking into consideration both the effects of water turbulence and the animals' internal states. By utilizing this covariance function in Bayesian filtering, we can make more accurate predictions about the animals' movement, their swimming speed, and their orientation in the water. Our proposed method outperforms the established methods for our demonstration scenario, proving its effectiveness in forecasting the swimming patterns of marine animals. Both the gas and stellar components of the galaxies were given high baryon densities, consistent with typical galaxy collisions at high redshifts. We ran a series of high-resolution, radiation-hydrodynamics simulations using the AREPO code with an internal resolution of 4,000, and in the absence of any external magnetic field, the outcome was a tumbling system with an irregular galaxy shape. This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in cloud-based databases, which we call update trend leakage. We contend that DP-Sync, a new protocol we develop, effectively mitigates this risk through the utilization of differential privacy. In DP-Sync, a user's partial updates are combined with noisy values to mask their individual update patterns, thus preventing the cloud server from obtaining any insight into these patterns while still enabling efficient and secure database maintenance. Re-identifying individuals across different cameras and time points presents a major challenge in surveillance due to the absence of labeled data. This problem is further complicated by the large number of unidentified individuals with no corresponding matches. To address this, we develop a novel approach called Extended Unsupervised Re-identification (EUR) that targets the re-identification of individuals in an extensive unsupervised environment. Our proposed method extends the basic self-supervised re-identification framework through contrastive training, allowing it to identify individuals by learning their distinctive features. To mitigate the risk of errors, we develop a procedure for validating and discarding unreliable identifications. Our experimental results demonstrate that our EUR approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in the existing re-identification challenges and surpasses the performance of a baseline method on a real-world large-scale surveillance dataset. Our work also shows the importance of considering the characteristics of unsupervised re-identification scenarios when evaluating the effectiveness of re-identification methods. Our EUR framework is particularly effective at re-identifying individuals in scenarios with a large number of unidentified individuals. New applications for pulsar timing arrays, specifically focused on identifying gravitational wave backgrounds produced by supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies, require extensive numerical modeling. This involves calculating the minute effects of GWB on pulsar spin phases, which in turn relies on precise numerical solutions to the Einstein field equations under stationary, axially-symmetric environments. Unfortunately, the usual approach to this problem, based on the Regge-Wheeler decomposition, encounters difficulties when trying to model PTA signals. This paper proposes an alternative strategy, using the Teukolsky equation to directly generate the necessary pulsar phase calculations. A key benefit of this method is improved efficiency, which can be particularly advantageous in case certain gravitational wave sources prove resilient against other PTA analysis methods. 

This paper is particularly concerned with certain extremely low-frequency GW backgrounds, which are produced by the movement of small black holes or intermediate-mass black holes in galaxy mergers. These sources are distinctive in that they generate GW signals at frequencies lower than the characteristic bandwidth of typical PTA signals. While the new approach has already been applied to two of these backgrounds, it is expected to be useful for a broader range of similar scenarios. 

The new approach to solving the Teukolsky equation, along with the detailed computational protocols for evaluating the associated pulsar phase residuals, are made available as open-source software, capable of being executed on both high-performance computing systems and personal computers. 

The new approach has already been applied to two specific scenarios: (1) an intermediate-mass black hole moving through a disk surrounded by an accretion disk, and (2) a small black hole moving through a group of star clusters. 

The resulting pulsar phase residuals produced by this new approach are available for download and use by other researchers in the field. 

The new approach offers significantly improved computational performance, with the ability to process complex models involving multiple objects moving through each other. 

The new approach can process models involving up to 10 objects moving through each other, and has been used to create pulsar phase residuals for over 200 different pulsar targets.

The nature of the pion, a fundamental particle involved in the strong interaction, has been the subject of numerous investigations aiming to clarify its nonperturbative characteristics. Primary considerations involve the parton distributions within the pion, particularly the spin-dependent distributions, which have been the focus of several studies conducted at quark mass zero. This paper seeks to expand our understanding by examining the two-correlator relation, which connects the unpolarized pion structure function to the nonlocal quark-quark and quark-gluon correlations in the lattice QCD, and to derive the unpolarized pion structure function from the latter in the continuum limit, utilizing data from lattice configurations with $2.1 \leq am_\pi \leq 3.4$. The study validates the two-correlator relation and provides the unpolarized pion distribution function for the momentum fraction $x$; this is the first time such a derivation has been made possible by the cumulative efforts of lattice QCD, Chiral Effective Theory, and perturbative matching calculations. The results obtained support the findings of previous studies conducted at quark mass zero and contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the pion's internal structure. The investigation described in this paper has been carried out within the framework of the CLQCD collaboration. The associated data has been shared publicly and is based on clover fermions obtained from configurations for full QCD simulations conducted at finite temperatures and zero chemical potential, using $N_f=2$ staggered flux multiplication. The underlying actions and parameters are listed in the paper's tables. The results presented in the paper have been discussed previously at the Lattice 2019 and HADRON 2019 conferences. We propose a new method to measure directional emission in microcavity lasers, focusing on the entropic characteristics of their intensity distribution. This approach is versatile and applicable to various directional emission patterns that can arise in these devices. We successfully employed this method to study and characterize the emissions produced by microcavity lasers with normal mode selection and those with mode selection broken, using theoretical models and numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that the entropic difference is an effective measure of the directional emission in these devices. Furthermore, this method is relevant to the study of directional emission in other systems and could be a useful tool for the analysis of future related research. Our research team previously reported on the phenomenon of spontaneous directional emission in microcavity lasers and identified the key factors that contribute to mode selection. Building upon this knowledge, we investigated and characterized the emissions produced by two types of microcavity lasers: one with mode selection broken and one with mode selection unbroken. In the latter case, we observed a higher level of entropic difference, indicating a more focused emission pattern. Additionally, we found that increasing the pumping rate in the device with mode selection unbroken led to an increase in entropic difference, but only up to a certain point. In contrast, the entropic difference remained constant in the device with mode selection broken, regardless of the pumping rate. This behavior suggests that there are optimal pumping conditions for achieving the most directed emission in devices with mode selection unbroken. In microcavity lasers with mode selection broken, the emission pattern is influenced by other factors, and changes in pumping rate do not affect the entropic difference. Furthermore, we analyzed the time-dependent behavior of the emission pattern in these devices. Our results show that the entropic difference remains constant over time in devices with mode selection unbroken, indicating that the focused emission pattern is a stable and enduring feature of these devices. In contrast, the emission pattern in devices with mode selection broken is more dynamic, and the entropic difference varies over time. This difference in time-dependent behavior could be exploited to study the fundamental properties of these devices over extended periods. Our research also explores the practical applications of microcavity lasers with directional emission in areas such as optical communication, biomedical imaging, and environmental monitoring. We demonstrate the feasibility of using these devices for high-resolution spatial distribution analysis. Our findings show that the focusable emission pattern in microcavity lasers with mode selection unbroken enables non-invasive detection of biological tissues, including living cells, and allows for clearer imaging of objects in scenarios where light is scattered.

Our analysis reveals that particle entanglement plays a key role in producing nonlocal effects in quantum systems. To illustrate this concept, we examine a single particle moving within a Young's interferometry setup, modified to include a beam splitter. By tracking the particle's motion, we identify an genuine nonlocal phenomenon - we call it single-particle steering. This phenomenon arises when the particle, after passing through the interferometer, is redirected based on the initial state of another, separated particle. We demonstrate that this effect cannot be achieved with local operations and classical communication. Furthermore, single-particle steering can be achieved even when the system is in a mixed state, and we propose an all-optical experiment to exemplify this nonlocal phenomenon. Additionally, we examine the relationship between single-particle steering and other nonlocal effects, including the violation of local realism and the distinction between different quantum states. Our findings underscore the significance of single-particle steering in understanding the nonlocal behavior exhibited by entangled particles. The integration of transportation systems and the growing number of interconnected vehicles through the Internet creates opportunities for enhanced safety, efficiency, and convenience. However, this setup also raises concerns over privacy and security in vehicle networks. Currently, existing solutions primarily address these issues with measures such as authentication protocols and encryption methods but often compromise efficiency for better security, which can impede the development and deployment of next-generation vehicle technologies.

On the other hand, emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, and the Internet of Things are transforming the education and training of safe and secure drivers by providing simulated experiences and promoting a culture of road safety. Nevertheless, these initiatives are hindered by limitations in resources, a lack of standardization, and difficulties in engaging drivers in training programs.

Recent research into Blockchain and Federated Learning demonstrates potential in creating secure and decentralized systems without compromising efficiency and privacy. Therefore, this paper conducts an in-depth review of the application of these technologies to vehicle networks, focusing on the development of secure, standardized, and decentralized systems for training safe and secure drivers.

With respect to education and training, this study reveals the advantages of Blockchain and Federated Learning in promoting a culture of road safety, engaging drivers through simulated experiences, addressing resource constraints, and resolving issues with standardization. Moreover, this paper also highlights the challenges and limitations in the implementation of these technologies in vehicle networks, citing problems with the decentralized decision-making process, the risk of decentralization, and the difficulties in achieving standardization.

Finally, this study presents an innovative Blockchain-enabled Federated Education Framework for Internet of Vehicles, which incorporates the use of Blockchains and Federated Learning in the training of safe and secure drivers. This proposed framework leverages the benefits of decentralized systems, while addressing the limitations and challenges mentioned earlier. This paper also outlines the design and key components of this new framework, including its decentralized decision-making system, secure and efficient architecture, and the ability to promote a culture of road safety. With respect to training, this study reveals the advantages of simulated experiences, while highlighting the difficulties in engaging drivers through these methods.

In terms of the training of safe and secure drivers, this research demonstrates the benefits of simulated experiences, while also identifying the limitations and challenges in this area. This includes the difficulties in creating effective and realistic simulations, the limitations in resources to support these simulations, and the difficulties in engaging drivers through these methods.

In conclusion, this study conducts an in-depth review of the application of Blockchain and Federated Learning to vehicle networks, while also exploring the development of secure, standardized, and decentralized systems

In this paper, we present a novel codebook creation approach and feedback encoding scheme for Frequency Division Duplex (FDD) systems. Our codebook development method is grounded in the principles of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and yields a highly efficient solution to the codebook design problem by formulating it as an online GMM learning process. This process allows us to leverage a significantly smaller amount of training data compared to traditional maximum likelihood estimation. Building on this codebook development method, we design a feedback encoding scheme that adapts codebook entries to the characteristics of the channel, resulting in improved performance. Our proposed approach and scheme are evaluated through numerical simulations, revealing substantial gains over state-of-the-art designs in the order of 10 dB in terms of spectral efficiency in FDD systems. Furthermore, we explore codebook size and feedback encoding time trade-offs, along with ideas for extending this work to Full-Duplex systems. Our results suggest that the GMM codebook design can provide significant enhancements to existing designs with relatively low computational complexity.

The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and onboard data processing systems before new space missions are launched, a portable GRB test tool has been developed. This portable device replicates various GRB scenarios using an electron linear accelerator and a gamma-ray detector system based on silicon carbide, and it also evaluates the detection capabilities of GECAM's GRDs. A thorough analysis of the test device's technical specifications and test results is presented in this paper. Specifically, an electron beam with an energy of 8.0 MeV and current of 20 mA is used to generate a full-angle gamma-ray flux of approximately 200 cnt/(s cm^2) at 1 m from the detector, which corresponds to an international system (IS) spectral peak energy of 0.8 MeV. Additionally, the capability of the data processing system to transmit data from the detector to the host computer via an Ethernet interface was verified. This test tool has facilitated the characterization of GECAM's GRDs at the Shanghai Institute of Spaceflight Control Technology and has helped prepare the detectors for integration into the flight units. Furthermore, this test tool has also demonstrated its utility in educating students and young researchers about gamma-ray detectors and data processing systems. Finally, this paper concludes with an evaluation of the test results obtained with the portable GRB test tool. This evaluation indicates that the performance of the gamma-ray detector system based on silicon carbide, which is part of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor, closely matches the requirements specified in the mission requirements document. This is evident from the spectral analysis of the data obtained with the detector system, which shows a clear power-law distribution with a characteristic photon index of -1.07, consistent with the standards for GRBs. Moreover, the detection capabilities of the data processing system, which is part of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor, were found to be more stringent than the requirements specified in the mission requirements document. Deep learning models like LSTM have revolutionized time-series data analysis, consistently outperforming traditional methods. Nonetheless, their extensive parameters pose a challenge for their practical application, particularly when equipped with large training datasets. To address this issue, this research proposes a novel, compressed LSTM model called HLT-LSTM, optimized for real-time video identification on embedded platforms. The HLT-LSTM model applies the hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition algorithm to streamline LSTM's considerable memory requirements and facilitate efficient training with small datasets. Human instructors frequently provide contextual feedback in the form of annotations to machine learning models, which are often restricted in their ability to process information due to considerations of computational cost, memory constraints, or categorization restrictions.  Despite the value of this feedback, it is often discarded because machine learning models are not designed to effectively utilize contextual information from annotations.  In this study, we explore the potential of enhancing machine learning via annotations by supplementing training data with additional contextual information.  Specifically, we investigate whether incorporating contextual information from annotations improves a machine learning model's performance on restricted data tasks in NLP.  The results of our experiments indicate that incorporating contextual information from annotations facilitates machine learning on limited data by equipping the model with a broader range of patterns to draw upon.  Interestingly, we find that the benefits of incorporating contextual information from annotations are more pronounced for models trained with limited data, while models trained on more extensive data datasets still benefit from the practice, although the gains are smaller.  Moreover, we discover that the advantages of incorporating contextual information from annotations are more evident when the constraints on machine learning models are imposed in terms of their capacity to process information rather than their classification choices.  The potential of this approach to increase the effectiveness of machine learning models in NLP is demonstrated through a series of experiments on CoNLL-SHF and Gigaword, covering tasks of text classification, sentiment analysis, and sentiment classification.  The code for this study has been made available online at https://github.com/AndreaCimino92/InfoEnhance.  The technical terms employed in this abstract are defined as follows: NLP: Natural Language Processing; ML: Machine Learning; RDL: Restricted Data Learning; PML: Pattern Matching Learning; FE: Feature Extraction; IA: Annotation Augmentation; IAE: Information Augmentation for RDL; ContextFE: Feature Extraction using Context; ContextIA: Annotation Augmentation using Context; BaselineIA: Baseline Information Augmentation; StrongModel: Strong Machine Learning Model; WeakModel: Weak Machine Learning Model; PMLModel: Pattern Matching Machine Learning Model; SimpleModel: Simple Machine Learning Model; MultiHeadModel: MultiHead Machine Learning Model; BigModel: Big Machine Learning Model; SmallModel: Small Machine Learning Model.  The study reported in this abstract has implications for the field of NLP, highlighting the value of contextual information from annotations as a means of enhancing machine learning.  This finding is significant in light of the difficulties encountered when machine learning models are trained on these annotations

Performing reliable simulations of many-body systems using a quantum computer is extremely difficult due to the difficulty of accurately evolving a corrupted quantum state. Evolution of the model space using the quantum imaginary time evolution method bypasses this issue, providing an unbiased estimate of the ground state energy and model space wave function. This approach also enables the simulation of systems in equilibrium with external fields. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method for systems with strong interactions and small particle numbers, such as nucleon systems, by comparing our results to conventional classical Monte Carlo modeling. Additionally, we outline the expansion of this approach to include multi-region simulations, enabling the modeling of systems with distinct model spaces, potentially including interacting fermions within these spaces. The proposed scheme facilitates the calculation of observables unique to specific model spaces or regions. We apply this concept to examples such as pairing interactions within model spaces and the study of quark systems in quantum chemistry, showcasing its broad applicability. The suggested model-space quantum imaginary time evolution algorithm is amenable to near-term quantum computing hardware, with potential extensions to multi-region simulations leveraging multiple quantum processors in the future. The future of this algorithm may involve optimizing its performance for full quantum tolerance through quantum cross-talk, which could yield even more accurate results. The proposed algorithm is currently being tested on the IBM Quantum simulator using approximately 250 logical qubits and approximately 500 parametrized gates for a single-shot simulation of 6 nucleons. The development of this algorithm is relevant to the broader quantum computing field, given its unique approach to managing quantum errors during simulations. The recently introduced quantum tolerance testing for this algorithm on small systems such as atoms and small molecules suggests that it may also yield accurate results when compared to classical modeling, further solidifying its relevance. The matrix element method's efficiency is examined for identifying Higgs boson pairs at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically for production of a Higgs boson and a W boson, followed by the decay of the Higgs bosons into b quarks and W and Higgs bosons. The analysis shows that the matrix method outperforms the fixed-cut approach in terms of identification efficiency, purity, and reconstruction accuracy of physical properties for all involved particles. The improvement in efficiency and purity is substantial, at more than a factor of ten. The matrix method also provides more accurate calculations of key observables, resulting in better distribution matching between signal and background. The time required for this method to process one event varies between 1.8 microseconds for the most basic configuration and 10.2 microseconds for a more detailed one, with the latter still considered real-time for the Large Hadron Collider's data volume. The paper addresses potential critics of using the matrix method for pair Higgs production identification, addressing concerns about radial tail rejection, over-training, and the computational time. This paper examines the non-linear Schrödinger equation under the influence of a potential that has a convex barrier in a limited area, with a focus on solutions that move quickly and expand. We show that, given certain conditions on the potential and initial wave function, these solutions will continue expanding indefinitely, with support expanding at a rate greater than the critical value determined by the minimum of the potential's lowest point and the sum of the square of the dispersion and the imaginary part of the Schrödinger equation's parameter. Additionally, given that the potential's lowest point is non-negative and the initial wave function is confined to a compact area, we find an explicit lower bound for the rate at which the solution's support expands. Furthermore, we establish that, under the condition that the potential's lowest point is non-negative and the initial wave function is highly localized, there exists a range of rates of expansion for which solutions with given parameters will continue expanding indefinitely, with support expanding at a specific rate greater than the critical value determined by the minimum of the potential's lowest point and the sum of the square of the dispersion and the imaginary part of the Schrödinger equation's parameter. The findings in this paper build upon previous work by B. Y. Wang and R. Zhang in the context of the linear Schrödinger equation. The method employed in this paper also yields a new proof for a related explosion result by M. Burq and G. Zhang in their study of the linear Schrödinger equation. To study the electronic structure of atoms or molecules, researchers typically use techniques such as laser spectroscopy, yet these methods are not suitable for detecting nuclear phases. This paper introduces a new technique, nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy, which utilizes resonant x-ray scattering to achieve this understanding. By harnessing x-ray pulses with controlled polarization properties, this method provides a direct connection between nuclear spin states and the spectral characteristics of scattered x-rays. This connection allows for the accurate measurement of nuclear phase through a combination of laser-induced fluorescence and x-ray scattering. This new technique's effectiveness is demonstrated using the specific example of $^{9}$Be, where x-ray scattering is used in conjunction with a laser field to accurately measure the phase associated with the hyperfine structure of the ground state. This technique is versatile and open to further development, as evidenced by the theoretical potential of using it to study nuclear phase effects in molecules. This study also highlights the capabilities of x-ray scattering in controlled atomic systems, revealing its sensitivity to atomic internal structure and phase. This understanding is expected to contribute to the development of new x-ray-based methods for precise measurements in atomic and molecular physics. This paper further shows that this technique can be employed in precise laser cooling, a process where the interaction between atoms and laser fields is optimized by considering the nuclear phase. A hybrid version of this technique, characterized by piecewise linear approximations for finite elements and piecewise constant approximations for boundary elements, is particularly effective in capturing the Darcy flux continuity across element boundaries. We investigate a prominent class of nonconvex matrix optimization problems that involve decomposing a matrix into fixed-rank components, under a specific constraint and objective function. By defining a suitable Riemannian manifold, we demonstrate that any local minimum or maximum of the problem corresponds to a stable fixed point of the gradient flow on that manifold. Furthermore, we establish that this gradient flow has a distinct geometric property, making it a geodesic convex program. We also identify general conditions and proof strategies for the convergence of certain algorithms targeting this type of optimization, as well as conduct an in-depth analysis of specific instances of this class of problems. By applying our framework to these instances, we obtain novel results, including a 64-process parallel computation of the Global Minima for the well-known Submodular Log Determinant problem, and an analysis of the convergence of Quasi-Newton methods for Matrix p, p-SDP, and Log Det Concave problems. This approach ensures the preservation of both charge and current continuity, as well as angular momentum, linear momentum, and spin. Consequently, derivatives of these quantities can be used to derive more complex properties, including magnetic dipole moment, orbital moment, and spin. Notably, the rapid multipole technique, an accelerated Jefimenko method variant, also maintains continuity of charge and current, linear momentum, and angular momentum. Nonetheless, the underlying differential equations of this method differ from those of the original Jefimenko approach, which has led to misconceptions regarding the rapid multipole technique's conservation properties. A detailed examination of the technique's differential equations has demonstrated that they are equivalent to Maxwell's equations, which, in turn, guarantee the conservation of angular momentum. Building on previous work by Gubser, we examine rotating operator segments in CFT2, using a specific unitary operator segment as an example. This unitary segment represents a rotating strip of finite width, bounded by two infinitely long straight lines. We aim to relate its behavior to holographically encoded information within AdS3 spacetime. Focusing on the dual description in Fefferman-Zamolodchikov Liouville theory, we use transformation properties and modular transformations to gain insight. Specifically, we leverage the existence of a dual gravitational description to infer how rotating operator segments interact with boundary points, likely influenced by gravitational effects such as gravitational waves. Nonetheless, this insight also provides a means to access these segments' properties without resorting to a full reconstruction of the bulk AdS3 physics. As a result, we are able to reconstruct the central charge for the dual CFT1 that arises from the intersection of this unitary segment with a dual unitary segment, now effectively reduced to a single point. Furthermore, we establish that the resulting dual CFT1 exhibits features of non-trivial topological order, characterized by an non-trivial modular S matrix and an entanglement central charge that is distinct from the conformal central charge. Ultimately, this understanding allows us to reinterpret previous findings related to co-adjoint orbits and holomorphic blocks within the AdS3/CFT2 correspondence. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be capable of differentiating between various primordial scenarios, including those involving the breakdown of scale invariance. Delensing - the process of removing primordial scalar modes induced by gravitational lensing - is crucial for achieving this level of understanding. By leveraging a machine learning-based lensing reconstruction technique, we've investigated its effectiveness in recovering primordial tensor modes. Our research indicates that a neural network trained on simulated data can successfully decode its input, and this decoding fails when the data is contaminated with artificial primordial scalar modes. To overcome this limitation, we developed a new framework that can train the network to prioritize lensing signal recovery, resulting in superior performance. Our findings show massive improvements in delensing efficiency, with a factor of ~3 when the neural network is trained to optimize lensing power spectrum estimation. This technique holds significant potential for enhancing future lensing analyses, particularly in studies of primordial tensor modes. To further demonstrate its utility, we applied this method to the COBE/Smolarch/ACBAR and Planck satellite data sets, yielding highly competitive constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio at zero wavelength, $r=0.021\pm 0.019$, which is more stringent than the current Protostar+Smolarch/ACBAR result. Additionally, we derived constraints on the delensing efficiency factor and the coherent primordial tensor fraction parameter, $f T / T \sim 0.017$.$ Moreover, this technique has implications for the expected performance of CMB experiments like CMB-S4. When considering the impact of foreground components on the neural network, we discovered that it can resist component confusion, yielding robust results across various models. To further examine this approach's applicability to upcoming experiments, we simulated CMB-S4 data and found that even without specifically removing the foreground components used in training, the delensing performance is comparable to that achieved with such removal. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established an intriguing link between geometric systems and classical invariant topology. Specifically, they demonstrated that the generating function for certain geometric systems equates to a universal expression involving Pontrjagin classes, which accurately captures the structure of the class $K$ functor. Our study delves into a precise interpretation of their groundbreaking result. We initially examine a standard form for generating functions in the context of graded algebra. We then apply this understanding to identify the universal expression for geometric systems as a form factor multiplied by a class that represents the class $K$ functor. We also establish that this universal expression can be represented through an iterated integral, drawing from the fundamental properties of the class $K$ functor. We conclude our exploration by presenting an illustrative example. In the process, we also derive an enumerative formula for the second Pontrjagin class, which aligns with a notable result by Kontsevich. Furthermore, we identify an intriguing connection between geometric systems and modular forms. We anticipate our findings to contribute to a broader theory that could reveal connections between geometric systems, modular forms, and the theory of motives. This investigation leads to the derivation of several significant results, including a uniqueness theorem for a specific type of nonlinear transport equation, the existence and uniqueness proof for a system of nonlinear transport equations on a compact domain with multiple stages, and a stability result for a nonlinear transport equation under weaker conditions than existing literature. Recent studies utilizing deep learning techniques for halo-abundance predictions from power spectrum information reveal that the cosmic web and density fields contain redundant information for predicting standard cosmological quantities, including matter density and halo mass function. However, the significance of incorporating the cosmic speed field (CSF) into these predictions is unclear. Our analysis indicates that the CSF's contribution is minimal when comparing its predictive performance to other cosmological fields and that its inclusion incurs a significant computational cost without improvements in halo mass function predictions. Notably, we find that the CSF's effect vanishes when considering the mass function within individual halos. In contrast, the mass function is influenced by the CSF on large scales, specifically at $10 < k < 10^3 h/Mpc^3$. Here, we demonstrate that this scale-dependent effect arises from the influence of instabilities on structure formation and suggest a simple, physically motivated filter to capture this effect in predictions made from power spectrum information. By applying this filter to our deep learning network, we significantly improve its performance when predicting halo mass function on small scales. Furthermore, we find that omitting the CSF improves the absolute percentage error (APE) of halo mass function predictions by approximately $10\%$ when considering all halos and $5\%$ when considering only massive halos. In contrast, the impact of the CSF on matter density predictions is negligible. In conclusion, we recommend removing the CSF from future N-body simulations to achieve computational cost savings without compromising the accuracy of predictions for standard cosmological quantities. In lieu of the CSF, we suggest using a physically motivated filter that can be applied to power spectrum information to improve the performance of deep learning networks when predicting halo mass function on small scales. In follow-up work, we explore the implications of these findings for model selection and validation and the identification of distinctive features in power spectrum information that capture the effect of structure formation on large scales. We demonstrate that the performance of our deep learning network is robust across different models and validation schemes and that the application of our physically motivated filter yields consistent improvements in predictions made from power spectrum information. In addition, we show that the effect of structure formation on large scales can be captured by considering the amplitude of perturbations on these scales, which modulates the development of instabilities and affects the mass function on small scales. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate the development of efficient deep learning simulations that accurately model the behavior of structure on large and small scales within our universe. We present a novel numerical approach for generating equilibrium configurations of rotating stars in general relativity, based on a reformulated energy functional that incorporates rotation effects. This formulation differs significantly from the conventional Carter-Lichnerowicz approach, allowing us to directly solve the complex Einstein field equations through the use of a conjugate gradient method, without requiring the derivation of semi-analytical equations. Our method is particularly well-suited for complex configurations, such as those involving massive rotating stars with neutron star companions, and we highlight the advantages of our approach over traditional methods, including a greater sensitivity to perturbations and a more efficient convergence, resulting in more accurate results with less computational demands. We validate our method by comparing our numerical findings with existing studies and demonstrate its applicability and computational efficiency using a range of rotational models, including stars with endogenous magnetic fields and stars in stable binary systems. Our approach represents an enhanced framework for examining the structure and behavior of rotating stars within relativistic theory, and it paves the way for a more comprehensive exploration of relativistic rotation effects in stars and the consequences of rotation on gravitational waves emitted during binary neutron-star mergers. Furthermore, our method has been incorporated into the new version of the relativistic stellar rotation code, known as RR4V. This new code, along with its code package, is publicly available for download at the specified URL. Recent machine learning advancements in document extraction have been impressive, yet they require an extensive amount of annotated documents to train models effectively. To mitigate this limitation, we've developed a document annotation tool called DocAnno, which streamlines the labeling process by leveraging both artificial intelligence and human insight. DocAnno's user-friendly interface is powered by a state-of-the-art machine learning model, allowing it to suggest precise annotations for each section of a document. Human annotators can then review and refine these suggestions in real-time, across multiple documents simultaneously. By combining human expertise with the machine learning model's capabilities, DocAnno significantly reduces the time and cost associated with annotating documents. Our research showcases the benefits of DocAnno through an evaluation of a document extraction model trained on financially sensitive documents, highlighting the importance of data quality in document annotation. Furthermore, we explore the concept of co-annotation, which enables multiple human annotators to work together on the same document in real-time, providing a potential avenue for future research and collaboration. Despite its potential, we observe a notable decrease in the quality of annotations when co-annotation is employed. To address this limitation, we propose a more robust approach called sequential co-annotation, which allows human annotators to work on documents in succession, while leveraging the machine learning model's suggestions. This approach demonstrates a notable increase in both efficiency and cost-effectiveness, while maintaining the quality of annotations. Our research and the DocAnno framework are relevant to any machine learning-based document extraction application that relies on annotated data, and we anticipate our findings to be applicable across a wide range of domains and use cases. Additionally, we believe that DocAnno's design and the co-annotation concept can be adapted to other visually rich data annotation tasks, such as video and audio data. Our research with the DocAnno framework also raises important questions regarding the interplay between human and machine intelligence, particularly in the context of sequential co-annotation. To address these concerns, we propose a theoretical model that simulates human and machine behavior during co-annotation, while identifying key parameters that influence the co-annotation process. This model can be used to predict the outcomes of co-annotation in different scenarios, while providing a foundation for further research on this topic. Overall, our research with the DocAnno framework underscores the significance of cost-effective data labeling, while highlighting the benefits of a collaborative approach between human and machine intelligence. The rapid spread of COVID-19 forced millions of people to work from home, leading to a significant reduction in human interaction in urban areas. This research examines mobile phone location data from a representative sample of the US urban population, tracing individuals' daily work, sleep, and exercise patterns, as well as their social connections with others in the same income bracket. We discovered a notable decrease in social distinctions during pandemic lockdowns, as people from all income levels reduced their physical interactions with others, adhered to curfews, and exercised more frequently at home. However, these uniform responses began to diverge over time, with lower-income individuals exhibiting less discipline in maintaining their scheduled work and sleep patterns, and also failing to sustain the increased exercise levels seen in other income groups. Consequently, lower-income individuals' reduced adherence to these habits resulted in a more significant decline in their urban interactions with others, ultimately widening the existing gap between lower and upper-income individuals in this regard. These findings suggest that lower-income individuals faced greater difficulties in adapting to the pandemic's new norms and may have experienced more severe lifestyle disruptions, consistent with research indicating that they have struggled more in navigating the pandemic's economic and health challenges. This research highlights the value of incorporating lifestyle factors into urban dynamics, demonstrating how individual behaviors can influence the way different income groups interact with each other in an urban setting. It also illustrates the utility of using aggregated, anonymized location data to study the pandemic's impact on urban ecosystems and related social phenomena. This study's findings on the pandemic hold broader implications for understanding the effects of other rapid, society-wide transitions on urban environments and human behavior. The formation of O-type stars remains an subject of great interest in the study of massive star formation, though the conventional view holds that such stars induce the destruction of their parent molecular clouds through intense radiation pressure and stellar winds. This thesis presents a novel approach to the problem by observing the [CII] line at 158 $\mu$m in a sample of seven protostars, including three massive protostars candidates, using the Hubble Space Telescope as part of the HIFI/HSPEC spectral mapping observations of the massive protostar RFQ G009.62+00.39. These observations enable the detection of gas at 50 km/s velocity shifts, as well as the identification of cloud structure and physical conditions. Furthermore, this research is part of a broader study on the [CII] line across the entire W51 giant protostellar complex. 

The massive protostar at the center of this cloud, with a luminosity of approximately 10^6 L_⊙ and a temperature of around 10^4 K, is surrounded by a disk with mass equivalent to ten times the mass of the Sun, as well as two large outflows that are around 10^4 years old and have widths of approximately 0.1 parsec. There is also evidence of a smaller protostar with a mass of around one solar mass located just 0.01 parsecs from the main protostar, as well as two separate cloud entities that are separated by just 0.01 parsecs and moving towards each other at a velocity of approximately 3 km/s. This finding could provide a solution to the problem of the early stages of massive star formation by creating a massive protostar through the merger of smaller protostars, as well as contributing to the total mass of the protostar through the accumulation of gas over time. 

However, recent observations using the Submillimeter Array (SAA) have revealed that this protostar, along with the smaller protostar it shares space with and a third separate protostar, is actually composed of two separate entities moving towards each other, which has led to a proposal of a protostar merger scenario. While this view holds that massive protostars can form through the merger of smaller protostars, as well as accumulating gas over time, it remains the subject of debate and further research is needed to fully understand the process of massive star formation.

For compact regions, we examine the endomorphisms of the local algebra generated by a given wedge-shaped region. These endomorphisms create a network of local observables, extending from the past to the future infinity. We investigate the consistency conditions under which these endomorphisms are coherent and consistent with the principles of local quantum physics. We establish a criterion for their consistency, which is represented by a cohomology class. We also identify the conditions under which these endomorphisms result in a consistent, locally adapted local algebra across all spacetime. We explore various examples of consistent networks of local observables, focusing on those that incorporate scalar fields and gravitational degrees of freedom, and we establish the conditions under which these endomorphisms lead to a consistent, locally adapted local algebra across all spacetime. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these consistent networks of local observables and the concept of local charge automorphisms. We demonstrate that any consistent network of local observables can be represented as a combination of these automorphisms, which are defined by the composition of two Longo-Witten endomorphisms. We also examine the composition closure property of these endomorphisms, which provides a new interpretation of the consistency conditions, and we identify the consistent networks of local observables as those whose underlying abstract representation forms a closed subgroup.
